#6601. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6600. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6599. 32 Makeup Gift Sets Every Beauty Lover Will Obsess Over

Somewhere between the first holiday party invite and the moment you realize November is already a quarter of the way gone, your gift list starts growing on its own. The good news? Presents from the beauty category make it a lot more manageable. They’re easy to shop, they’re hard to get wrong, and everyone in your life could use a few more of them, whether they like to admit it or not.

It can be as simple as a lipstick in a case they’ll want to show off, or as big as the LED mask they’ve had in their shopping cart for months now. And there’s plenty to love in between, from skin care they’d never splurge on for themselves and makeup gift sets to a beauty tool or two that turn the bathroom into something close to a visit to the facialist.

Every year, the same people are the hardest to shop for: the mom who insists she doesn’t need anything, the sister with impossibly specific taste, the friend who has genuinely tried it all. This list has them covered, along with a few names you’ll probably add later. Keep scrolling to shop the best beauty gifts and thank yourself in mid-December when you’re crowned best gift giver ever.

The best makeup gifts are the ones most people wouldn’t buy for themselves, like a designer lipstick in a case nice enough to leave out on the vanity, or a set of minis that finally gets someone to try a brand they’ve been curious about. This year’s holiday sets lean right into that, with limited-edition shades and packaging that looks just as good on a dresser as it does wrapped under the tree. Whether the person on your list does a full face every morning or rarely gets past mascara, there’s something here for them.

It’s hard to go wrong with Chanel, and this set is all about the small details that make someone feel put=together. Tucked inside a limited-edition white pouch with a soft, knitlike texture, it includes the Rouge Coco Baume Satin tinted lip balm, which goes on sheer and builds to lipstick-like color with a few more swipes, plus one of the brand’s hand creams and a bottle of the Le Vernis nail polish in the classic shade Ballerina.

For the person who treats their makeup bag like an accessory, this one comes in a sleek metallic clutch that’s chic enough to carry on its own. Inside, there’s Prada’s Pradascope mascara for lifted, clump-free lashes; the refillable Monochrome lipstick in Tiepolo, a soft, diffused matte finish; plus two lip balm refills in Universal and Astral Pink that keep lips comfortable for up to 24 hours.

For the friend who always has their trusty lip liner handy, you can’t go wrong with this set. Makeup artist (and Vogue Beauty Board member) Fara Homidi’s Smudge & Contour pencils are a cult favorite, designed with a creamy, almost balmy feel, so they glide on without dragging, and can be smudged out with a fingertip or sculpted into perfection with a makeup brush. The brand’s holiday trio comes in three neutrals, a cool beige, a taupe, and a deep brown, covering everything from a barely-there line to a deeper, more defined lip.

If someone on your list always runs late to holiday parties, they’re in luck, because we’ve uncovered the perfect gift for them. Gucci Westman picked the four products she’d reach for with only a few minutes to get ready, and all four come in mini sizes that slip easily into an evening bag. A cherry red blush stick and a rosy-taupe highlighter take care of the cheeks, while a charcoal eye pencil and Westman’s buildable mascara handle the eyes, so the whole look comes together fast.

In our opinion, skin care is one of the easier things to gift, since almost everyone has a routine, and most people are quietly hoping someone will hand them the moisturizer or serum they’ve been too practical to buy for themselves. The best picks this season either upgrade a step someone already loves or introduce them to a brand they’ve been curious about, and a few come in packaging nice enough that the box doesn’t even need wrapping.

Sulwhasoo has built its name on ginseng, and this set is the easiest way to see why. It includes the brand’s full-size Concentrated Ginseng Rejuvenating Cream along with smaller sizes of the matching eye cream, serum, and cleansing foam, so the whole routine is covered from start to finish.

This is the moisturizer to give the person who has tried everything. Dr. Diamond’s HYDR/O is a sheer cream that sinks in quickly but delivers serious hydration, thanks to a long list of hyaluronic acids, ceramides, and squalane that help strengthen the skin barrier over time.

Dieux’s got loyal fans for a reason, and this kit pairs two of its most popular products in one, reusable and decorative tin. The full-size Deliverance Serum helps calm redness and soften the look of wrinkles and dark spots, while a mini Instant Angel Moisturizer locks in moisture and leaves skin dewy enough to wear under makeup. Both are fragrance-free and gentle enough for sensitive skin, so it’s an easy gift even if you’re not sure what someone’s routine looks like.

For the friend who loves a Sunday night face mask, this set is basically a week of spa nights in one box. It includes five of 111Skin’s sheet masks, each one targeting something different, from hydration and brightening to depuffing, plus a lifting mask for the neck. Each takes about 20 minutes, and at a $161 value, it’s a fun way to try the brand’s bestsellers and find out which one is best for you.

Beauty tools tend to be the gifts people secretly want most and are least likely to buy themselves, mostly because the price tags make it hard to justify. That’s exactly what makes them such a good present. This year’s picks bring the kind of treatments you’d normally book at a dermatologist’s office or a facialist into the bathroom at home, from LED masks and laser caps to a hydro-facial that takes about 10 minutes.

Currentbody’s LED masks already have a cult following, and the Series 3 is its most advanced yet. It packs 750 LED bulbs and six different wavelengths, including red and near-infrared light for firmness and fine lines, and blue light for breakouts. The brand’s MyDose technology works out the right treatment for your skin, and there are four preset modes if you’d rather not think about it. A touch-screen controller with a countdown timer makes it easy to stick with, which matters, since LED works best with consistent use.

For anyone dealing with thinning hair, this is one of the most serious tools you can give them. The Capillus Spectrum looks like a regular baseball cap, but inside, it uses red and infrared lasers to stimulate hair follicles, and it’s FDA-cleared to treat hereditary hair loss in both men and women. It only takes six minutes a day, and the cap shuts itself off when the session is done, so it’s easy to wear while you answer email or make coffee.

Think of this as a facialist that fits in your hand. HigherDose’s just-debuted wand pairs a cold laser with red, near-infrared, and blue LED light, so it can help firm and smooth fine lines on one setting and calm breakouts and redness on another. A cooling attachment swaps on to depuff under-eyes and sculpt along the jawline, and most sessions take 10 to 15 minutes. It even comes with a travel case, plus minis of the brand’s peptide serum and facial mist to prep skin first.

For the person on your list who splurges on a biweekly or monthly facial, the Shark Beauty FacialPro is most likely sitting high on their wish list. An easy way to unclog and clean pores plus infuse skin with powerful ingredients like hyaluronic acid, this gift takes its owner into the driver’s seat, giving them the power of visiting their favorite spa right at home.

Hair gifts are a safe bet for almost anyone, since even people who barely think about their routine still have a shampoo they’re loyal to or a styling tool they’ve been eyeing for months. From a splurge-worthy straightener that skips the hot plates entirely to travel-size sets that are perfect for stuffing into a carry-on, there’s something for the person who does their own personal blowout every morning and the one who simply wants their strands to feel soft.

Anyone who’s ever waited for their hair to dry before reaching for a flatiron will understand the appeal here. Dyson’s Airstrait dries and straightens at the same time, using airflow instead of hot plates, so you can go from towel-dried hair to a sleek, finished look with one tool. It has three heat settings and a separate mode for touching up dry hair, and the arms lock together so you can rough-dry your roots first. It’s a splurge, but it cuts out an entire step of the routine.

If holding a round brush and a dryer at the same time has never worked out for you, this is the fix. Wavytalk’s thermal brush works on dry hair, so you get the volume and bend of a blowout from a single tool, with five heat settings up to 420° F and a ceramic barrel that heats evenly. Negative ions help keep frizz down, and since it’s dual-voltage, it’s easy to pack for trips abroad.

As frustrating as it can be, you can’t reach your hair goals if you don’t repair damage first. If your giftee has been trying to assuage breakage, heat damage, or dry and brittle strands, Redken’s Acidic Bonding collection is like the golden ticket. Powered by Bonding Care Complex and citric acid, these products are formulated to reinforce weakened or broken bonds for smoother, stronger hair—and even protect hair color from fading.

For the person in your life who’s always on a plane, this set from RŌZ packs a full routine into carry-on-friendly sizes. The masterwork of celebrity hairstylist and Vogue Beauty Board member Mara Roszak, this set includes the Foundation Shampoo and Conditioner, the Santa Lucia Styling Oil for frizz and shine, and the Milk Hair Serum, a leave-in that works whether you air-dry or blow-dry. Plus, everything is sulfate-free and smells as good as it performs.

Yes, buying perfume for someone else can feel like a gamble, since what smells amazing on you might not work on them at all. There are two easy ways around that—you can go with a classic that almost everyone likes, or you can give a discovery set and let them find a favorite on their own time. We’ve rounded up a short list of both, so whether they’ve been wearing the same scent since college or still haven’t found their signature, there’s something here that’ll end up in their perfume collection.

If you’re shopping for someone who already loves Coco Mademoiselle, this set is a no-brainer. It pairs the full 3.4-ounce bottle with the Twist and Spray travel size, so there’s one for their vanity and one for their bag, all in limited-edition holiday packaging. The scent opens with bright orange, softens into jasmine and May rose, and settles into patchouli and vetiver. It’s easy to see why it’s become one of Chanel’s most recognizable fragrances.

For someone who loves fragrance but hasn’t found their signature yet, this set from Hermès makes the search a lot more fun. It includes minis of four of the house’s best-known scents: the warm, spicy Eau des Merveilles, the ginger-and-tuberose Twilly d’Hermès, the green, mango-tinged Un Jardin sur le Nil, and the luminous floral Jour d’Hermès.

If someone on your list loves a perfume that makes them stand out, put this one at the top. Merit’s New Wave is an extrait, made with nearly 30 percent fragrance oil, so it lasts a lot longer than most eaux de parfum. It starts out a little spicy from pink pepper and gets warmer and sweeter as it wears, with orange blossom and honey up front and vanilla and incense underneath.

Not sure whether they’d like something light or something a little more intense? This set lets them try both. It comes with four minis of Cartier’s La Panthère, an eau de toilette, two eaux de parfum, and the parfum, and they all share the same mix of gardenia and soft musk. The eau de toilette is the lightest of the bunch and works for daytime, while the parfum is deeper and better for a night out.

Some of the best gifts aren’t about what goes on your face but about how you feel day-to-day. Wellness picks make sense for the person who’s always trying to sleep better, drink more water, or finally figure out why they wake up tired, and they tend to get used every single day. These four are easy upgrades that will fit right into your giftee’s routine, whether they’re a total wellness devotee or just curious.

Most people filter their drinking water without thinking twice, but the water they shower in every day rarely gets the same attention. Jolie’s shower head swaps in for your regular one and filters out chlorine and heavy metals, which can leave hair dry and dull and skin feeling tight after a shower. Over time, they should notice softer hair and clear, glowing skin becoming the norm.

Oura’s new Ring 5 is about 40% smaller than the last one and made from lightweight titanium, so it’s easy to forget it’s on—perfect for the person who has been complaining about their sleep for years. Each morning, the app shows how well they slept, how stressed their body was, and how they’re recovering. The battery lasts up to nine days, and the charging case holds about a month of backup power, so there’s no need to pack a charger for a long weekend away.

If anyone you know is obsessed with their oral hygiene, getting them the Rolls-Royce of toothbrushes will keep you slated as the ultimate gift giver forever. Polish, prestige, and next-generation cleanliness make Philips’s latest in dental technology the ideal present for those who like to get five stars every time they visit the dentist.

For the person who needs a little bit of calm in their life and has getting bigger muscles on their resolution list, the vibration plate is the perfect contribution toward their 2027 health goals. This version from HexaPlate uses side-to-side oscillation to tamp down an active nervous system if you just want a little bit of relaxation or to challenge the body when doing squats, lunges, or push-ups.

La Mer is one of those brands people love but rarely buy for themselves, so this set is a smart way in. For under $100, you get four minis worth $250 in total: the brand’s lightweight Moisturizing Soft Cream; the Resurfacing Treatment, a gentle liquid exfoliator; the Renewal Oil; and The Concentrate, a serum made to calm stressed, irritated skin. Everything comes zipped inside a velveteen case, which works just as well for travel once the minis are gone.

This is a great gift for anyone who’s been eyeing red-light therapy but isn’t ready to spend hundreds on a mask. The set pairs True Botanicals’ Pure Radiance Supreme Eye Cream, made to firm and smooth the skin around the eyes, with a small red-light wand that you glide along the orbital bone after applying the cream. The wand shuts itself off after two minutes, so there’s no guessing how long to use it on each eye. Worth $215 in total, it’s another Nordstrom exclusive.

If you know someone who’s obsessed with anything vanilla-scented, this set from Summer Fridays will go straight into their bag. It includes the brand’s cult-favorite Lip Butter Balm in Vanilla in full size, plus travel sizes of the Body Butter Balm and the Sunlit Vanilla Eau de Parfum, which smells warm and a little like dessert. The perfume slides into an exclusive key-chain holder, so it can clip onto a purse or keys for touch-ups throughout the day.

Byredo’s Bal d’Afrique has a way of turning up on just about everyone’s vanity, and once you’ve smelled it, it’s easy to see why. If there’s a fellow fan in your life, this mini set lets you give them the whole ritual without the full-size price tag. It includes the fragrance, a body wash, and a body lotion, so the scent carries from the shower through the rest of the day, plus a tiny key chain filled with the perfume that clips right onto a bag for touch-ups on the go.

When winter hits, body care quickly becomes one of the most practical gifts you can give. Between the cold air outside and the heaters running inside, skin tends to feel tight and dry by mid-December, and most people don’t realize how much they need a good body oil or scrub until one is in their hands. These sets cover every step, from a scrub that buffs away dry patches to a rich cream afterward, and a few come with scents nice enough that they double as fragrance. They’re also an easy pick when you’re not sure what someone’s skin type is, since nearly everyone could use a little extra moisture this time of year.

For the friend who reads ingredient lists and actually wants to see results, Osea’s holiday set is a smart pick. It starts with the brand’s body scrub, which buffs away dry, dull skin and leaves it glowing, followed by its algae-infused body oil to lock in moisture and help skin look firmer and more elastic over time. And the dry brush, for daily lymphatic drainage and sloughing away dead skin, will remain useful long after the body-care products run out.

Fit for the king or queen in your life, Flamingo Estate’s Jasmine Damask Rose Bathroom Set takes the bathroom experience to the next level. It includes hand wash, a scented candle, and a bar of soap that indulge the senses in the rich and luxurious fragrance note that David Lynch himself deemed “intoxicating.”

If there’s a Salt & Stone fan on your list, this three-piece set is an easy way to stock them up for less. It comes with the brand’s bestselling scent in three minis—a fragrance, a body wash, and a deodorant—so they can layer it from the shower through the end of the day. The body wash is made with nourishing botanicals that keep skin from feeling dry, and the deodorant lasts up to 24 hours, which makes the set as practical as it is nice to smell.

Soft Services’ bestselling hand cream was made for the nightstand, and now there’s a version for the desk too. The new Lumelo Weightless Hydrator is a great pick for your office bestie or the friend who’s always applying hand cream between meetings. Instead of the rich texture of the original, it has a light, gel-like feel that sinks in fast, so it’s easy to work into a midday break without leaving fingerprints on your laptop.

#6596. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6595. Palmer Harding Spring 2027 Ready-to-Wear

As much as anniversaries are cause for celebration, they naturally also prompt introspection. For Palmer Harding, this season marks 15 years in operation—and their 60th full collection. These are milestones well worth raising a glass to for any independent brand, not least one that has weathered the market instabilities and headwinds that we’ll take your understanding of as a given.

The past year has prompted particularly significant operational developments for the brand – a noteworthy one being the opening of a retail space within its East London studio. In part prompted by the widely attested decline of global wholesale retail, this direct-to-consumer pivot has allowed for an intimate atmosphere that, Matthew Harding says, “feels almost like when we first started; there’s more interaction between us, the clothes and the customer.”

This, in itself, became something of a prompt for their latest collection; less a nostalgic ‘greatest hits’ offering, more a zeroing in on the pieces they’ve seen resonate. “It’s very much a collection about refining and celebrating our key pieces, translating them into new silhouettes, new categories,” Harding adds.

Contemplating what exactly those pieces were didn’t take them too long. “When we actually hunkered down and said, ‘Okay, what are we about?’ The answer was cotton shirts and shirt dresses. When we find a shape, let's just really hammer it home," Palmer says, holding up a hefty poplin button-down with articulated pleating along its oversized sleeve, creating an easy, boomerang bend. First introduced two seasons ago, here, the aptly-named “Intention” shirt returns across a gamut of plain and striped cottons, and as a full-length dress imbued with a satisfying, fanning swish.

Elsewhere, the asymmetrically-hemmed “Super” shirt—“one of our hero pieces that really launched us way back when,” Palmer recalls, “but that we haven't had in the collection for a long time”—showcases the duo’s knack for sculptural cut and drape with its tie-front and cape-like back. Though the piece that showcases that most intriguingly is what Harding dubs the “Precision” shirt, which features origami-like criss-cross pleating at the waist to create a line that skims the form.

There are, granted, more than crisp cotton shirts and shirt dresses on offer here. A denim riff on the “Intention” silhouette stands out, as does a ruby satin dress with swooping poet sleeves. Their insistent focus on their chosen fabric and garment, however, is in itself somewhat allegorical of the alchemical formula that’s spurred their trajectory over the past 15 years. “There's something really wonderful about taking what’s seen as a boring, everyday fabric and elevating it in a really sculptural way,” Palmer says. “The result is something this blend of something that's really understandable, but also very special.” A decade and a half on from setting out with that mission, the eclectic array of women willing to journey far beyond London’s well-trodden luxury shopping lanes to try and buy their wares in person proves that still holds true.

#6594. Salted Coffee Custard Pie

If you can’t be fussed with making coffee and dessert after a big holiday dinner, consider this twofer instead. The silky, sliceable, cool custard is rich and intense with two kinds of coffee, while the oatmeal crust is a tweedy-textured study in contrast. It’s prebaked to mitigate sogginess but doesn’t require pie weights. Mascarpone keeps the whipped cream firm and fluffy for a full 24 hours.

Don’t be tempted to skip the cold-brew concentrate. You don’t want regular cold brew, and definitely not brewed and cooled coffee from your coffee machine at home, no matter how fancy. The concentrate (highly recommend Grady’s Cold Brew Coffee Concentrate) is consistent every single time with exactly the right strength to stand up to the dairy and eggs in the filling.

Cook’s notes: This pie requires a 9"-diameter deep-dish pie dish.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

Place a rack in middle of oven and preheat to 350°. Butter pie dish with unsalted butter. Pulse 2 cups (180 g) old-fashioned oats, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) dark brown sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a food processor until oats are coarsely ground. Drizzle in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled; pulse just until mixture comes together. Transfer to prepared dish (such as East Fork Ceramic Pie Plate); wipe out and reserve food processor. Press crust firmly and evenly across bottom and up sides of dish with a flat-bottomed measuring cup. Bake until golden and surface looks dry, 25–30 minutes. Transfer crust to a wire rack; reduce oven temperature to 325°.

Pulse 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. instant espresso powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in food processor until no lumps remain, about 1 minute. Add 3 large eggs, ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and pulse until smooth. Add 1 cup cold-brew coffee concentrate and 2 cups heavy cream and pulse until well combined.

Pour custard into crust (it’s okay if crust is still warm). Bake pie until edges of filling are set and slightly puffed but center still wobbles a little when gently shaken, 40–50 minutes (filling will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack; let cool at least 3 hours, or, preferably, chill 12 hours.

Using an electric mixer, beat ½ cup mascarpone, 4 Tbsp. granulated sugar, remaining 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ⅔ cup heavy cream, and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract in a medium bowl until soft peaks form. Spoon whipped cream mixture over pie; swirl lightly to create divots and peaks.

Just before serving, dust with instant espresso powder if desired; sprinkle generously with flaky sea salt.

Do ahead: Pie (without espresso powder and sea salt garnishes) can be made 1 day ahead. Cover loosely and keep chilled.

#6592. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6591. I Just Learned How to Apply Leave-In Conditioner Correctly

Leave-in conditioner tends to be the product people buy right after a great salon blowout, convinced it’s the secret behind how soft and smooth their hair looks leaving the chair, only to get it home and find it doesn’t behave the same way at all. A big squeeze rubbed in everywhere like hand lotion usually ends with roots that look greasy by the next morning, and ends that still catch on the brush. Before long, the bottle is collecting dust at the back of the bathroom cabinet. Most of the time, though, the formula isn’t what went wrong.

“I always want a leave-in conditioner to give the hair what it needs without losing its movement,” says celebrity hairstylist Paul Perez, co-founder of Flore. That’s hard to pull off if most of the product ends up on your scalp, or gets watered down before it ever reaches your ends, which is why he’s quick to add that “placement matters just as much as the product.”

A lot of it comes down to things that happen at the salon without anyone really noticing. Your stylist wrings out your hair before reaching for any product, for instance, and that alone keeps a leave-in from sliding right off wet strands. They also tend to dry your hair a section at a time, starting underneath, which is a big part of why it comes out so smooth, and it’s exactly the kind of step that’s easy to rush through at home when you’re trying to get out the door.

Below, hairstylists and a trichologist explain how to apply leave-in conditioner from start to finish, along with the products they’d reach for at each step.

A leave-in can only do so much on hair that’s still coated in yesterday’s dry shampoo, which is why the process starts in the shower. “The best way to use a leave-in conditioning product is on clean hair after washing,” says celebrity hairstylist Wendy Iles, founder of Iles Formula. Work your shampoo into your scalp, since that’s where oil and product tend to build up, and let the lather rinse through your lengths on its own rather than scrubbing the ends. Conditioner should go on your mid-lengths and ends, where hair is older and drier, and it only needs a minute or two before you rinse it out with lukewarm water. It’s worth taking your time with that rinse, because any conditioner left behind will stack up with your leave-in and weigh hair down, something fine hair tends to feel first. If you use a lot of styling products, swapping in a clarifying shampoo every week or so will keep buildup from getting in the way.

If your hair always feels a little dry by the end of the week, start with a good hydrating shampoo. This one from Moroccanoil cleans without that squeaky feeling, thanks to argan oil, red algae, and vitamins A and E. It’s sulfate-free and safe on color-treated hair. Use less than you think is enough—it’s concentrated, so a splash of water turns a small amount into plenty of lather.

Yes, we agree $67 might be a lot to spend for one bottle of shampoo. But this one is a cream, not a gel, and it washes more like a conditioner than a cleanser. Moringa and baobab oils soften hair that’s dry, colored, or heat-styled, and it doesn’t leave finer strands flat.

Not every shampoo has to fix something. This one is for hair that’s healthy but looking a little more dull than usual. Apple, matcha, and kale clean without stripping, and the shine shows up after a wash or two. It’s also free of sulfates and silicones, so it won’t build up, even after multiple uses.

This is the kind of conditioner that makes a regular Tuesday shower feel like a salon visit. Gold Lust is made for hair that’s dry, damaged, and a little over it, and it’s packed with argan oil, shea butter, biotin, and niacinamide to bring back softness and slip. There’s even UV protection, so your color hangs on a little longer. If you’re in a rush, even two minutes through your mid-lengths and ends will do wonders. But if your ends are feeling a little bit on the crunchier side, give it the full five, and your comb will glide right through.

This is where most people go wrong, since it’s tempting to apply leave-in to hair that’s still dripping. “When hair is oversaturated, water occupies the internal spaces of the strand (the cortex). This dilutes your product and causes it to slide right off the cuticle,” explains trichologist Jay Small, co-founder of Arey.

Instead, squeeze the water out with your hands first, then wrap your hair in a soft towel made for hair, like Arey’s Hair Wrap, until it feels damp rather than soaked. Before you reach for the bottle, run your fingers through your hair and notice which parts feel dry or rough, because, as Perez points out, “your ends may need more conditioning than the newer hair closer to the roots.” Iles starts with about “a nickel or quarter size,” rubbed between the palms and smoothed “from the mid-lengths to the ends,” keeping it off the scalp “to keep your hair from looking oily.” If your hair is fine, Perez suggests spraying the leave-in into your hands first instead of directly onto your head, then running a wet brush through to spread it evenly.

If your hair drinks up moisture and still looks thirsty, keep this one by the sink for tiny refreshes throughout the week. It’s a light, milky mist made with organic pomegranate oil, and it hydrates for up to 72 hours while protecting against heat up to 450°F. There’s a natural UV filter in there, too, which comes in handy on beach days when you’ve had a little too much heat. Fine hair should keep it to the mid-lengths and ends, while thick or textured hair can go roots to tips.

This is the leave-in for people who swear they hate leave-ins. It sprays on as a fine mist and dries without any film, so fine and medium hair doesn’t fall flat. Virtue’s Alpha Keratin 60ku helps calm frizz and split ends, and there’s a bit of UV protection, too. Spritz it on damp hair right when you get out of the shower, comb through, and style. Bonus points for the citrus and tea notes, which are the perfect treat early in the morning.

If brushing out your hair feels like a fight, start here. This spray is all about detangling, and Living Proof says it makes hair nine times easier to comb through. It’s weightless, protects against heat up to 450°F and UV, and uses time-release peptides to keep hair soft all day. Spray it from roots to ends on damp hair, focus on the knots, and comb through.

Olaplex took its cult conditioner and made it into a leave-in version, allowing all of us to count on its bond-building technology whenever needed. The gel-cream uses the brand’s bond-building technology to repair hair and seal split ends, and it doubles as a heat protectant up to 450°F. Olaplex says it adds 12 times more moisture after one use, and you can feel it in your ends. Work a small amount through damp hair before styling, and if your hair is fine, start with less than you think.

Drying your whole head at once might feel faster, but it’s usually how you end up with smooth layers on top and frizz hiding underneath. “If your hair remains in clumps or clusters, it will be very difficult for individual strands to dry evenly,” says Small. Perez sections hair before he even applies any product, “so you reach the underneath layers, rather than putting everything on the surface,” and the same idea works when you pick up the dryer. Spray on a heat protectant, clip the top half of your hair out of the way, and start at the nape, working in sections about as wide as your brush. Keeping the nozzle pointed down the length of your hair and the dryer moving the whole time will give you more shine and less frizz once you’re done.

If your blowout always frizzes out by lunch, this is the step you’ve been skipping. It’s a milky cream that smooths every strand before the dryer even comes out, then keeps humidity from undoing all your work. The best part about this primer is that it also protects against heat and cuts down on breakage. To use, comb a hazelnut-size amount through towel-dried hair and blow-dry as usual.

A styling cream that doesn’t weigh you down? It actually exists surprisingly. Verb’s Ghost Prep protects up to 450°F, tames flyaways, and adds shine, all from a dime-size amount. Moringa oil and green tea extract do the heavy lifting. Not heat styling everyday? Dab a little on your ends for a glossy, air-dried finish for when you’re skipping tools. And at under $20, you won’t feel bad going through a bottle or two every few months.

Anyone who’s ever given up on a blowout halfway through will appreciate this one. Bumble and bumble’s spray is designed to cut blow-dry time in half, and fewer minutes under the dryer means less heat damage over time. All the credit goes to the brand’s Honey Protective Complex, which smooths frizz and helps prevent breakage, plus UV filters for sunny days. Mist it over damp hair before drying, focusing on the crown and the back of your head.

If your blowouts never look quite as smooth as the salon’s, this balm is a good place to start. It goes on silky and melts into a cream as you work it through damp hair, so it’s easy to spread evenly without overdoing it. Mustard seed oil helps block humidity, kiwi oil keeps hair hydrated, and it protects against heat up to 450°F. Warm a small amount between your palms, run it through, and blow-dry as usual—your style should still hold its shape on day two.

This is the step that makes a blowout look polished rather than almost there, since a drop or two of serum or oil smooths the flyaways your brush left behind, adds shine, and helps keep frizz from creeping back by mid-afternoon. It’s easy to overdo, especially with fine hair, so warm a small amount between your palms and press it into your mid-lengths and ends, keeping it well away from the roots. You can always add a little more later, but there’s no quick fix for hair that ends up looking greasy.

IGK’s Crybaby is a serum-in-oil, which sounds fussy but just means it sinks into hair instead of sitting on top of it. That’s why it can smooth frizz and add shine without the greasy finish some serums leave behind. Coconut oil softens dry ends, prickly pear extract boosts shine, and there’s UV protection to help keep color from fading. A small amount on damp or dry hair goes a long way.

For a serum that just gives you that je ne sais quoi, reach for this cult favorite from Philip Kingsley. It’s a triple threat, working to tame frizz, delivering tons of shine, and also leaves the hair smelling lovely. Safe for color-treated hair, just a small amount is all you need for a “finishing touch.”

Ouai’s oil earned its cult following for good reason. Firstly, it’s light enough for fine hair, but it still smooths frizz, seals split ends, and leaves a glossy finish. It’s got just about everything you need— protects against heat up to 450°F, hydrates so hair never feels dry, and can go on before a blowout as well as after. Work one to three drops through wet hair and let it air-dry, or smooth it over dry hair after styling to calm flyaways. It smells like violet and gardenia, which doesn’t hurt either.

Yes, it’s a splurge, but this is the kind of oil that makes your entire routine feel more luxurious. Sisley’s blend of botanical oils adds serious shine and softness without weighing hair down, and a couple of drops is all you need, so even a pricey bottle can last you a while. Smooth them from the mid-lengths to the ends on damp hair before styling, or on dry hair as a final polish.

How much leave-in conditioner should I use?

Less than you probably think, and it’s better to build up slowly than to start with a big squeeze. Small points out that it’s easy to go overboard when hair is still too wet, which “can cause you to over-apply the product without realizing it until the hair is dry, forcing you to start the entire process over.” Perez suggests starting small, then pausing to see how your hair feels before adding more. “The hair should feel supple and easy to handle, without feeling over-saturated,” he says. “Give a dry section a little extra attention instead of adding another layer everywhere.” Thicker, coarser, or curlier hair will usually need more product than fine hair, but the same rule applies either way.

Can I skip conditioner and just use leave-in conditioner?

For most people, it’s best to use both, since a rinse-out conditioner and a leave-in don’t do quite the same job. Your regular conditioner softens and detangles in the shower, while a leave-in adds a lighter layer of moisture and protection that stays on through styling, which is why Perez applies leave-in only “after washing and conditioning.” There are exceptions, though, and they usually come down to the product itself. “Repair treatments such as K18 Molecular Repair Mask require a different sequence,” Perez explains, which means shampooing “without conditioning first,” towel-drying, and applying the treatment before waiting “four minutes before combing or adding other products.” If you’re not sure, the directions on the bottle will tell you everything you need to know.

Is leave-in conditioner good for your hair?

Used the right way, yes, especially if your hair is dry, damaged, or prone to tangling. Wet hair is at its most fragile, and as Small notes, “the wetter your hair is, the more vulnerable it is to mechanical breakage,” so the extra slip from a leave-in makes brushing much gentler. That’s also why Perez recommends detangling “from the ends upward” with your fingers or a wide-tooth comb, aiming for “even coverage without pulling or repeatedly brushing fragile wet hair.” Many leave-ins also add heat or UV protection, which he says “provides a natural UV barrier.” The only real downside is using too much, so start small and focus on the ends.

#6588. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6586. Fall Harvest Minestrone

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Our fall harvest minestrone trades summer’s vegetables for autumn’s produce. Break out the slow cooker!

You may be familiar with the usual cluster of summer vegetables in classic minestrone, but any Italian will tell you that real minestrone changes with the season. Italians like to prioritize whole, nutritious, in-season produce—especially those living in Italy’s blue zone, where some of the longest-living people eat minestrone every single day.

As we dive into fall, we’re taking our classic minestrone recipe with us and giving it a couple of tweaks. Our fall harvest minestrone ditches the zucchini, green beans, parsley, basil and spinach, and reflects what’s growing in the garden right now: sweet potatoes, onions, kale, sage and rosemary. We included Italian sausage, too, to enrich the broth and add a big boost of protein—enough for this fall soup to officially be considered dinner.

In a large skillet, cook the sausage over medium heat until it’s no longer pink, six to eight minutes, breaking it into crumbles with a wooden spoon. Drain the liquid from the skillet, then transfer the meat to a 6-quart slow cooker.

Stir in the beef broth, sweet potatoes, canned tomatoes, kale, onion, carrot, garlic, sage and rosemary. Cook the minestrone, covered, on low until the vegetables are tender, five to six hours.

Editor’s Tip: The sweet potatoes should be fork-tender before moving on to the next step.

Stir the pasta into the minestrone. Cook everything, covered, on low until the pasta is tender, 20 to 25 minutes longer.

Ladle the soup into bowls and serve. If desired, top the fall harvest minestrone with Parmesan cheese, red pepper flakes or fresh sage or rosemary.

Allow leftover fall harvest minestrone to cool completely to room temperature in under two hours. Transfer the soup to an airtight container and store it in the fridge for up to four days.

Yes, you can freeze fall harvest minestrone. Let the soup come to room temperature in under two hours, then ladle it into freezer-safe, airtight containers. Freeze the soup for up to two months. Thaw it overnight in the fridge before enjoying it again.

Yes, you can make fall harvest minestrone gluten free. Buy a box of good gluten-free pasta and make sure the Italian sausage is gluten free, too. I like to cook the gluten-free pasta separately when I suspect I’ll have leftovers. I add the pasta to individual bowls, then top it with the soup. Gluten-free noodles will absorb too much broth overnight, breaking down and becoming mushy.

The fall harvest minestrone has everything: vegetables, carbs and meat. It doesn’t really need anything else, but if you want to stretch the meal a bit, serve the soup with cornbread, biscuits (I love our garlic bread biscuits) or slices of crusty sourdough bread. Something like a vinegary salad will cut the richness a bit and bring in fresh flavor.

#6585. November’s Bake Club Is a Triple Feature of Holiday Pies

We’re Jesse and Shilpa, senior editors and the resident bakers of the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. We love to bake—some might even call us obsessive—and we love to talk about all the hows and whys and what-didn’t-works that come with it.

Think of the Bon Appétit Bake Club as a book club, but for baking. Each month we share a brand-new meticulously tested recipe. Bake along with us, share your wins (or your fails—we’ve all been there), post pictures, ask us your pressing questions. We’re creating a community of confident, curious bakers who find just as much joy in the process of baking as the final results.

First, and most important, save each month’s recipe and bake it! You’ll find all of them below.

Join the Bon Appétit Bake Club chat on Substack and we’ll take you behind the scenes of our recipe development process.

Post and share photos of your beautiful bakes on Instagram using the hashtag #BABakeClub.

Share feedback and ask us questions in the Recipe Notes section of the recipe page in the Epicurious app. We read every comment and look forward to talking with you about butter, sugar, and more.

Send your baking questions to [email protected] for a chance to be featured on our podcast. Each recipe’s episode goes live at the start of the following month on the Bon Appétit podcast feed.

To celebrate pie, the iconic food of this American holiday (move over, turkey), we’re bringing back our trusty flaky-as-a-croissant crust that debuted in 2022. It has since become the only pie dough we use in the Test Kitchen—and in a room full of pro cooks, that’s a ringing endorsement. This year it’s the base of two recipes: a single-crust Cranberry Meringue Pie that will teach you all about blind baking and impress your loved ones with its towering slices, and a lattice-topped Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie whose double crust shows off all those buttery layers encasing lightly boozy caramel-draped fruit. Want homemade pie without making your own dough? We didn’t forget about you! Our Salted Coffee Custard Pie has a press-in oatmeal crust and a silky custard filling gilded with an airy layer of mascarpone-whipped cream.

Imagine a Parker House roll having a tryst with Asian-style milk bread and a classic French croissant—that’s the essence of salt bread, a.k.a. shio pan in Japan and sogeum-ppang in Korea. Each soft bun holds a rich secret: a nub of salted butter bundled within the shaped dough. The little pat of fat melts in the oven, pooling on the baking sheet to effectively fry the bottom crust, yielding a crisp, savory shell akin to something you’d find in a patisserie. I like to tear it in half to revel in the buttery, hollow center, then unravel each flaky layer, just like a croissant. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

Is it even fall if you haven’t been apple picking? And have you even been apple picking if you didn’t end the day racing to the farm stand selling still-warm cinnamon-sugar doughnuts? Our latest recipe is designed to recreate that experience—apple-studded dough, a hint of grease, a jolt of sugar and spice—without waiting for yeast to rise.

For those unfamiliar with karpatka, a.k.a. Carpathian Mountain Cake, let us enlighten you. Traditionally, two disks of tender, airy pâte à choux house a layer of pastry cream lightened with whipped cream or crème mousseline. This version ditches the classic filling for a no-bake cheesecake (!) ribboned with homemade plum jam. It’s make-ahead-friendly and endlessly fun; just the thing to keep the summer vibes going a little longer.

This sunflower yellow cake with an alluring bounce is Bake Club’s midsummer stunner. Fresh (or frozen! I don’t mind) corn blended with a can of sweetened condensed milk and our defining ingredient, sweet rice flour, makes up the bulk of the batter. The end result is a textural masterpiece with gentle resistance and slight elasticity that tastes like buttered corn, toasty coconut, and nutty caramel all at once.

If a tomato sandwich, pizza, and flaky pastry started a band, these tomato galettes would be their first hit single. Start by making a black-pepper-spiked pie dough, which needs no specialty equipment to bake up crisp and layered. Each little round is filled with a dollop of garlicky Parmesan and herb mayo, which acts as a barrier between each little galette’s juicy tomato slice and delicate pleated crust. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

Lemons are a powerful ingredient. So why miss out on their full potential by only using their juice and zest? That was the thesis behind these bars. By blitzing up two whole lemons into the curd, then straining out the pulpy bits, we keep lemon’s most exciting qualities: the bitterness of the pith, the essential oils of the skin, and of course, the acidity of the juice. Think Lemonhead candy. It’s everything I love about classic lemon bars with the volume turned up to a reckless decibel level.

Last year, for deputy food editor Hana Asbrink’s birthday, I made a strawberry roll cake filled with whipped cream and tiny jewel-red strawberries. It was an immediate hit and we decided right then that it belonged in Bon Appétit Bake Club. With fluffy cake, vanilla-bean-flecked cream, and juicy berries, it’s a dream dessert, tailored for this joyful season filled with new blooms and tender asparagus. Roll cakes traditionally require a complex series of steps when it comes to shaping, but this version utilizes an oil-based chiffon sponge, making it particularly easy to roll with no cracks and no heartbreak.

After last month’s cheesy biscuits, we’re going back to our dessert-loving roots and baking chocolate cake. But not just any old chocolate cake—this is a malty, brawny loaf imbued with Guinness stout. The crumb is tender beyond belief because of how you mix the batter. You’ll combine the dry ingredients, then rub in the butter by hand, until it practically disappears. This mimics a technique called reverse creaming and prevents excess gluten from forming. And there’s no special equipment, like a stand mixer, required.

A biscuit warm from the oven, split open so the steam rises to meet you, rivals the pleasure of an exalted loaf of homemade bread, all for a mere fraction of the effort (and wait time). This month’s recipe is packed with cheese and zhuzhed up with Old Bay seasoning. These biscuits are tall and layered like a lasagna, thanks to a quick and dirty lamination technique not unlike croissants. You don’t need any special equipment for these, but I highly recommend availing yourself of a nice bench scraper. It makes shaping the dough so much easier. Chris recently handed me a set from Gestura and I’ve been loving it because it’s small but sturdy, with thoughtfully curved edges and a minimal handle.

With a few pantry staples and a little time, this recipe yields a dozen delightfully chewy bagels that rival the most beloved of NYC shops. The trick? A two-step process: The bagels are first boiled, then baked. This dual approach gives them their signature chew, tanned sheen, and pleasantly dense (not tough) interior. And for a little fun: You can top these bagels with just about anything you like. Some of our favorites are furikake, Parmesan, sesame seeds (classic), and flaky salt.

This bake is inspired by Black Forest cake, a Bavarian dessert defined by its layers: chocolate cake, cream, cherries, and kirsch, a cherry brandy. Over the years it spread far beyond its woodland origins, to countries like India, Fiji, the Philippines, and the Caribbean Islands. One bakery in Chennai, India, where I grew up, made tall triangular slices, a treat my parents brought home if we did well on our school tests. Pavlovas are prone to crack, weep, or turn soggy and chewy. The key is in the ratio of sugar to egg whites. Two parts sugar to one part egg whites (by weight, of course) gives you a sturdy, crisp, snow-white pavlova.

Designed to maximize the ratio of sticky, gooey insides, arguably the best part of the pastry, this giant cinnamon roll was received with joy almost every time I made it. A little instant vanilla pudding mixed with cinnamon sugar mimics the ooey-gooey texture of mall-famous cinnamon roll filling, thanks to the modified food starch it contains. It’s purposefully large enough to cut into slices like a cake, but if you’re like us, you won’t be able to resist tearing it apart with your bare hands. Nor should you.

For those unfamiliar with the old-school pageantry of this French pastry, let us enlighten you: A Paris-Brest is a giant wreath of pate à choux (a foundational pastry dough) that puffs and expands dramatically in the oven. This version swaps the traditional praline mousseline filling for a banana-peel-infused (yes!) diplomat cream (just a fancy term for pastry cream lightened with whipped cream) and layers it with candied nuts and slices of banana. Everything good about Southern banana pudding, just in a flashier, French package.

Turn on the AC, because this month we’re making a lovely, homey pie. It’s everything good about summer (fruit! leisure! long days!) tucked away in a crisp, flaky crust, lightly scented with cardamom, and topped with a brown sugar streusel. There are some powerful learning moments in this bake: How to make a crust that will never fail you. How to select the best fruit for a pie. Why it’s important to precook a high-moisture filling so your pie crust is crisp rather. And perhaps the hardest and most important lesson of all: How long to wait before you dig into your pie ( it’s longer than you think).

This is no squishy sandwich loaf, but rather a big, browned boule studded with fresh jalapeños and chunks of cheddar. It’s ultra-savory and just a touch spicy. For those who might be intimidated by homemade bread (we see you!), think of this recipe as an intro course. It’s made with instant yeast, so it comes together quickly, without having to fuss over finicky active dry yeast or sourdough starter. And you don’t have to knead it; a few quick folds is all it takes.

This month we’re making Hummingbird Cake, an imposing icon from the American South. It’s a storied dessert with an interesting history that involves a Caribbean island, possibly a bird, and a magazine that’s over five decades old. If you’re unfamiliar, think of it as a banana version of carrot cake, full of nuts, spices, fruit, and cream cheese frosting.

The tang of cultured dairy from sour cream makes these scones stand out, keeping them moist but not claggy. And with that addition, channeling coffee cake became the natural next step. With clusters of streusel on top and a cinnamon sugar swirl within, these are scones that anyone will love.

Millionaire’s shortbread is the ultimate show-off bake. Our version went through about 10 rounds of testing until every detail was just right. The base of these bars—a simple, ultra-tender shortbread—gets a special upgrade: toasting a bit of the flour beforehand. This lends a deep nuttiness, almost like coffee, without any extra ingredients. The caramel takes a hybrid approach, bolstering caramelized sugar with sweetened condensed milk, so you get a bittersweet flavor with a sliceable texture. The final layer combines chocolate with butter for a mirror-like shine and fudgy bite.

The key to this pistachio cake’s tender crumb and mowed-grass green hue? A blender. It does all the hard work for you, decimating the nuts into a coarse flour and evenly distributing the dry ingredients (no sifting needed). This cake is satisfyingly hefty and moist thanks to the pistachios’ natural fat content, a combination of melted butter and oil, plus a pearlescent lemon glaze.

It’s easy to see the appeal of Basque cheesecake—dramatic visuals aside, it’s astonishingly easy to make. You don’t need a crust, or a water bath, or the long, slow cook of a New York–style cheesecake. The trick lies in cooking it hot and fast, much like pizza or steak, resulting in a cheesecake of epic contrasts, deeply caramelized on the outside while remaining quiveringly soft inside. I’ve added buttery mascarpone and a not insignificant amount of instant espresso to the batter to mimic another custardy classic, the iconic tiramisu. Topped off with a rosette of cocoa-dusted cream, it is two desserts for the effort of one.

Our pizza recipe meets you where you are: It can come together in fewer than 4 hours and is adaptable to an overnight rest. You don’t need a stand mixer, a clunky baking stone, or a specialty oven. And you’ll still get a world-class pie. The decidedly untraditional two-step cooking method (stovetop plus broiler) is a game changer, guaranteeing a puffy crust with enviable char (or leoparding, as the pros call it). To make dough-handling easier, we highly recommend a flexible bowl scraper.

This one-bowl cake has olive oil in both the chocolate cake and the ganache-like frosting. It’s a low-effort, high-reward recipe. And if there are any leftovers, thanks to that olive oil, the crumb will stay moist for days. Using Dutch-process cocoa powder gives this cake an intense chocolaty flavor. Our go-to brand for pretty much anything baking-related is Guittard Cocoa Rouge. It has a bold, concentrated complexity without any of the dull chalkiness common in other brands.

This project bake screams autumn. The perfect follow-up to apple picking, it’s a fruit-studded beauty, drenched in a tangy cider caramel and using almost half a gallon of apple cider. Make sure to use a 12-cup or larger Bundt pan for this recipe. Using a smaller variety can result in the dough proofing out of the pan. Nordic Ware actually invented the Bundt pan, and we love their version for its sturdy construction and even heat distribution.

#6584. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.
