A 2016 satellite photo shows Hurricane Madeline and Hurricane Lester heading straight toward Hawaii's Big Island. When viewed from above, the twin cyclones and the surrounding clouds look eerily like a giant smiley face.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's in the photo? Hurricane Madeline (left) and Hurricane Lester (right)

Which satellite took the photo? Suomi NPP

This eye-catching satellite snap from a decade ago shows a pair of hurricanes barreling toward Hawaii. The clouds swirling around the twin cyclones make them look eerily like the eyes of a pale face smiling up at space. The sight appears even spookier when viewed on a weather map (see below).

The surprisingly symmetrical storms — Hurricane Madeline (left) and Hurricane Lester (right) — were the 14th and 13th named storms, respectively, during 2016's Pacific hurricane season, which is tied for the sixth-most-active year on record, with 22 total named storms.

Madeline peaked as a Category 4 storm on Aug. 30, reaching maximum wind speeds of around 130 mph (210 km/h). Lester also briefly became a Category 4 storm on Sept. 1, reaching a maximum speed just below Madeline's, but it quickly weakened to Category 3.

On Aug. 30, the day after the image was taken, Madeline was just under 400 miles (650 kilometers) from Hawaii's Big Island, while Lester was around 900 miles (1,450 km) behind on the same trajectory, according to NASA's Earth Observatory. At the time, meteorologists were uncertain whether the pair would hit the island.

The Central Pacific Hurricane Center later issued a hurricane warning for the state of Hawaii, saying that Madeline, in particular, would pass "dangerously close to the Big Island," according to the Earth Observatory. However, neither storm ended up making landfall. (In the photo, the Big Island is obscured by reflected sunlight, known as a sunglint, on the left side of the image.)

When viewed on a radar-based weather map, the hurricanes look like they are staring up into space even more.

Madeline eventually passed south of Hawaii on Aug. 31. However, by then, it had been downgraded to Category 1. Lester passed north of the Big Island on Sept. 2 and came within around 130 miles (210 km) of Honolulu, before sharply turning northward, where it petered out.

Although neither hurricane made landfall — meaning the eye of the storm did not pass over a landmass — they still caused high winds, heavy rainfall and strong surf across the state.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Despite being in the middle of the corridor where most Pacific hurricanes form, Hawaii's islands have surprising good luck in avoiding the supercharged storms.

For example, in 2025, Hurricane Kiko was similarly spotted from space bearing down on the island state. But like Madeline and Lester, it suddenly changed course and weakened at the last minute.

Hawaii usually manages to dodge the worst effects of hurricanes for two reasons. First, the islands are surrounded by a near-constant area of high pressure on their eastern side, where most hurricanes come from. Second, strong winds often blow eastward across the islands, according to FOX Weather. These factors create a sort of invisible shield around the islands, causing storms to skirt around them.

While hurricanes almost never make landfall in Hawaii, they often come close enough to trigger strong gusts of wind on the islands.

However, given the recent rise in extreme weather events across the globe — caused by human-caused climate change — as well as changes to regional weather patterns, the islands may not stay so lucky forever.

For example, in August and September, two hurricanes — Lowell and Lala — skimmed unusually closely past the island of Kauai, causing a significant amount of damage to power lines, boats and other coastal infrastructure. Researchers think the ongoing "super" El Niño, which officially began in May and has already caused record-breaking sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, may be partially to blame for these storms, according to The Guardian.

A 2016 satellite photo shows nearly a dozen, surprisingly pronounced dark spots swirling in the clouds over Heard Island in the Indian Ocean.

A 2021 satellite photo shows an unusual series of concentric cloud rings that appeared directly above an erupting volcano on La Palma in Spain's Canary Islands.

A 2015 satellite photo captured a series of stunning "von Kármán vortices" swirling off islands in the Atlantic. It is one of the best examples of this meteorological phenomenon ever seen.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6580. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6577. The Best Teriyaki in Seattle

Who serves the best gorditas in Mexico City? Or Baltimore's can't-miss crab cakes? Welcome to Taste of the Town, where we call on a local expert to share the best versions of one of their city’s most iconic foods. Here, we explore Seattle’s take on teriyaki.

Seattle’s entire teriyaki universe exists because of one man, a pioneer of chargrilled chicken thighs. In 1976, Toshi Kasahara opened a restaurant serving lightly marinated and grilled chicken, glazed in a blend of soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and sugar. This wasn’t any teriyaki you’d find in Japan, but a cheap, filling, flavor-packed translation aimed at a working-class city still unaware of the tech boom on the horizon.

Kasahara established and sold about 30 shops over the years, and copycats began copycatting. Teriyaki became ubiquitous, the Japanese name concealing its hometown heritage. Some locals don’t even realize teriyaki joints are a Seattle thing—that is, until they move elsewhere and try to find one.

Kitchens with Vietnamese roots began dishing up teriyaki alongside steaming bowlfuls of pho. Many spots still specialize in a classic interpretation, typically served with scoops of rice, some fried gyoza, and iceberg lettuce bathed in a thin mayo dressing. Enterprising Korean immigrants embraced teriyaki and opened their own outfits, adding bulgogi to the menu and gochujang to the chicken’s marinade.

The forward march of time, trends, and real estate prices means there’s sadly no longer a teriyaki business every few blocks. Those that remain include a few clunkers: Many have succumbed to shortcuts, serving sad chicken in gloopy, way-too-sweet gravy, which obscure the dish’s appeal to outsiders. But find a place still making its own sauce and blasting thighs on high heat, delivering bits of caramelized char that balance its teriyaki sweetness. Then you’ll understand.

Local wisdom dictates the best shop is the one closest to you, but here are eight greats, new and old.

Toshi Kasahara’s original restaurant, now long shuttered, was the archetype of a Seattle-style teriyaki spot—a spare cafeteria-like space with a streamlined menu built around Kasahara’s iconic chicken. Just a sprinkling of these shops still exist, but today only one is the real deal: a take-out operation deep in a Mill Creek strip mall. It’s open just a few hours in the evenings, with the 77-year-old Kasahara at the grill. He’s tweaked his methods slightly over the years, but his chicken is just as juicy and smoky as ever. No one in Seattle does it exactly like Toshi, but his sons do farther afield. One runs a Toshi’s food truck in San Francisco; the other is opening a Toshi’s outpost this winter in his father’s hometown of Ashikaga, Japan.

Hawaii has its own relationship to teriyaki. When restaurateur Matthew Parker opened his ode to the teriyaki counters that fueled his first 20 years in Seattle, he looked to his family’s roots in Oahu—specifically to huli huli chicken. That dish inspires Grillbird’s glossy house sauce, sweetened just enough with pineapple juice and ketchup. There’s no iceberg salad here; sides include mac salad and marinated cucumbers, dishes standard to plate lunch, Hawaii’s answer to the meat-and-three. Purists can grouse about how teriyaki shops should be old-school in every sense, but I welcome Grillbird’s modern touches, like online ordering and a mostly gluten-free menu. Grillbird’s original West Seattle outfit occupies a former Pizza Hut, which feels just right for this utilitarian dish. A second location in Phinney Ridge operates alongside sister concept Salad Party, for those looking to get their greens in.

When the Lee family lost the lease on their longtime teriyaki restaurant, the new location they’d scouted came with a catch: The strip mall that housed it already had a teriyaki shop. So matriarch Yoo-Mi Lee camouflaged her teriyaki menu with dishes from her Korean heritage and influences from the years the family lived in Brazil. Be thankful for that other teriyaki business, because Tá Jóia’s highly specific Brazilian-Korean-teriyaki remix is so vibrant and delicious, it could (should!) be a national fast-casual restaurant chain. Feijoada, a hearty slow-cooked black bean stew made with pork, bacon, and sausage, fits right in next to bulgogi, while the kitchen’s spectacular teriyaki hides in plain sight under the moniker “spicy chicken bowl.” It’s the chicken teriyaki of your hottest, most chili-spiked dreams, brightened with a scoop of pico and a drizzle of creamy house cilantro sauce.

No matter which member of the Kim family is behind the counter here, chances are they will offer you tea while you wait for your order. If the hospitality is great, the food is even better. Chicken teriyaki looks like it came off a photo shoot, deeply juicy with properly charred edges. It’s chicken that needs no supporting cast, but with so many combos on the menu, it’s fun to compare how the gingery sauce hits different proteins including beef, pork, prawn, or tofu. (If you’re exceedingly hungry, go for the formidable triple combo, which delivers chicken and beef teriyaki, golden-fried gyoza with a flaky, blistered exterior, and fragrant mounds of fried rice.) Teriyaki lovers are especially protective of Rainier Teriyaki since its late owner, Hansoo Kim, was tragically killed during a 2023 attempted armed robbery; the family banded together and reopened the restaurant in his honor.

Most people show up at Fremont’s busy donburi shop craving its chirashi bowl, but the chicken teriyaki imagines what Seattle’s signature dish might have looked like if it actually hailed from Japan. Butterflied thighs with the lightest of marinades come straight off the grill to be dressed with a sauce that’s thin by Seattle standards, but nonetheless lands a careful balance of savory and sweet. I appreciate this subtler rendition of chicken teriyaki, which complements an otherwise traditionally Japanese menu of rice bowls. Granted, people don’t usually crave Seattle teriyaki for its subtlety; add a dose of the house chili oil for texture and kick. Fremont Bowl is a kiosk-driven take-out machine, but the dine-in vibes are friendly, provided you can find a free table.

Ask a local about their favorite teriyaki shop, and chances are high it’s this been-there-forever counter next to a laundromat not far from Lake Union’s north end—not to be confused with other very similarly named Seattle teriyaki practitioners, including one on this list. A high ratio of dark soy makes for a standout sauce, while the thin mayo-based salad dressing plays well against the crispness of the fresh iceberg lettuce. The kitchen even uses an old-school mold to press rice into a pleasing half-football shape. Many teriyaki shops also have chicken katsu and egg rolls on the menu, but the versions here are standouts for their nongreasy crispy exteriors. The tables are mostly waiting zones for people ordering takeout, destined for a lunch in Gas Works Park, the nearby brewery taprooms, or just back to the surrounding tech offices. Come hungry: Portions are huge, even by generous teriyaki shop standards.

Nikko is busy most of the day, feeding a bustling lunch rush, teenagers after school, and evening take-out crowds. That turnover means teriyaki that’s always fresh, swiped with sauce that’s more soy than sugar and thick without verging on gummy. Jong Kwon and his family have run this West Seattle staple with warmth for more than two decades. Step inside the narrow shop and you’re transported back to Seattle’s era of peak teriyaki, a simpler time when one ordered off pictures on the wall rather than QR codes and the cashier remembered your name.

Clamshell take-out containers are so inherent to the teriyaki experience that nobody asks if you want your food to go, they generally just assume you do. But visit this Georgetown favorite (no relation to I Love Teriyaki) and you’ll witness a rare sight: Diners eating off actual plates. After a three-year closure following a fire, owners Don and Eva Lo rebuilt the original building (once a KFC) into a shiny new space. Aromas of grilled meat hit you from the parking lot, and the cheerful dining room is usually full. Skip the newish teriyaki burritos, and run, don’t walk, to the short ribs teriyaki, so smoky and tender that you might almost be tempted to bypass the chicken altogether. Almost.

#6576. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6575. Countdown to Christmas with Snoopy! The Best Peanuts Advent Calendars

The Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar is both a beautiful luxury gift for loved ones and a nostalgic yearly tradition for families.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Here at Taste of Home, we know all too well that Advent calendars are no longer just for tots. In fact, some of the top-selling picks among our readership over the last few years include wine calendars and other boozy options. Not to mention the bestselling Bonne Maman Advent calendar, which has been voted one of our favorites for three years running! But when it comes to collectible calendars that double as unforgettable gifts, nothing impresses us quite as much as the Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar.

That’s right! The brand behind the iconic Spice Village now has Advent calendars. And yes, the Peanuts Advent calendar is just as gorgeous and nostalgia-filled as you’d imagine. Here’s my experience unboxing this assortment of adorable ornaments. Warning: spoilers ahead!

Boasting 25 ornaments crafted in Lenox's signature porcelain, the Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar is a luxury Advent calendar unlike any other.

The Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar isn’t just your average Christmas countdown. It’s a luxury Advent calendar that unfolds to reveal 25 doors, each housing its own adorable ornament. Because these are made from Lenox’s signature  premium porcelain, they’re meant to be enjoyed season after season. That makes this Advent calendar an extra special gift for Peanuts fans. It also makes a fun yearly tradition for families! Don’t forget to put on A Charlie Brown Christmas as you hang them on your Christmas tree!

This collector’s calendar comes with 25 different tree hangers, each boasting either an iconic wintery scene from the comic strips or one of our favorite classic characters. In total, there are 13 characters and 12 scenic snowflakes, all of which sit at around two inches tall. And these bite-sized heirlooms aren’t found anywhere else—you can only get them inside the Advent calendar, making them a thoughtful gift for collectors.

My experience unboxing the Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar was truly magical. Even before I opened the first door, I was struck by the packaging. While simple, the shiny red box looks classy and expensive. It also feels nice and hefty—a nod to the precious porcelain ornaments nested inside. Once you loosen the gold clasp, the calendar folds open like a book to reveal 25 doors, and each opens to reveal a figurine or snowflake nestled in a protective foam cushion. I love that the box is protective enough to reuse for storage once the season ends, too!

From Lionel to Peppermint Patty to Charlie himself, each of the character ornaments offers extraordinary detail. Despite the small size, they’re slightly heavy, so you can tell they’re also high-quality. Among the figurines are also several iterations of fan favorite puppy dog Snoopy partaking in holiday traditions and lounging on his light-wrapped doghouse.

Even the snowflake ornaments offer their own holiday charm. Each one is carefully painted with a miniature scene from the wintery comic strips. Among the art are ageless, captivating sequences of the gang gathered around a lighted tree, Lucy performing on ice skates and mischievous Snoopy tangled up in a string of vibrant Christmas lights among many others. Adorning each hanging loop is a festive tassel, giving the ornaments a little added flair.

Whether you plan on giving this one as a gift or want to keep it as a holiday heirloom, it’s truly a special collection that the whole family can enjoy. It’s also the perfect way to signal the most wonderful time of the year is here!

While we absolutely love the Lenox Peanuts advent calendar as a yearly tradition, it’s not exactly child-friendly (without parental assistance, that is). For folks seeking an alternative Advent calendar for kids that still offers the same Peanuts charm, we love this Peanuts puzzle Advent calendar. An experimental medical device uses a tiny amount of electricity to spark a chemical reaction and remove extra sugar from the bloodstream.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An experimental medical implant that removes excess sugar from the blood has shown promise in treating diabetes and obesity in tests with lab mice.

Coupled with a continuous glucose monitor, which tracks blood sugar levels in real time, the tiny device is designed to adjust blood sugar levels according to a patient's needs. It does so using a chemical reaction powered by electricity. In the mouse experiments, it prevented sudden insulin spikes and promoted fat loss.

The implant, described Oct. 22 in the journal Science, could offer a completely new way to treat diabetes and obesity, study co-author Martin Fussenegger, a professor of biotechnology and bioengineering at ETH Zurich, told Live Science in an email. His team is now working toward testing the device in additional lab animals, and eventually, humans.

About 790 million people have type 2 diabetes globally, and over 1 billion have obesity. People with obesity often have insulin resistance, in which cells don't respond to insulin well and can't take in the sugar they need from the blood. At first, the body makes more insulin to compensate, but eventually, it can't keep up; this sets the stage for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes. About 90% of people with type 2 diabetes also have obesity or are overweight.

At the same time, chemical reactions in the liver convert the extra glucose in the blood into fat stores, contributing to further weight gain.

Current treatments for these conditions focus on either lifestyle changes, such as diet and exercise, or long-term medications such as metformin, which lowers blood sugar, and GLP-1s, which reduce appetite to promote weight loss. But Fussenegger and colleagues wondered if they could target the glucose directly.

They designed an inch-long reactor that converts glucose into a harmless byproduct, called gluconate, through a controlled chemical reaction triggered by tiny amounts of electricity. This transformation takes place at an electrode coated with gold and platinum nanoparticles embedded within a graphite felt.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Crucially, the reaction occurs only when the device receives sufficient electricity, so the glucose removal can be switched on and off by controlling how much power is supplied to the implant.

The device is wireless and is both powered and controlled from an ordinary smartphone. The phone emits low-level radio frequency energy, which the implant's electronics then convert to a stable DC current to activate the reaction. Combined with a glucose monitor, the device detects high blood sugar and then sends feedback to the smartphone, which then adjusts the amount of power transferred to the implant.

"In principle, this enables the device to remove more glucose when [blood sugar] levels are elevated and reduce its activity when glucose returns towards the desired range," Fussenegger said. "The objective is to create an autonomous system that continuously adapts to the patient's metabolic needs."

In the mouse study, the implant was combined with a continuous glucose monitor, which provided updates on blood sugar levels to a phone that controlled the device.

The team tested this self-regulating medical device in mice with both diabetes and obesity. Over six weeks, the mice fitted with the implant had much more stable blood sugar levels than the untreated mice did. They also lost an average of 10% of their body weight.

Because the mice's glucose was consistently maintained within normal levels, the body's metabolic chemistry shifted toward fat burning, while the on-off regulation of the glucose-removal reaction prevented the mice's sugar levels from falling below safe limits.

It's an exciting proof of concept, Fussenegger thinks. However, "one important challenge is demonstrating that the device can convert sufficient quantities of glucose in a human while maintaining long-term safety and catalytic efficiency," he said. In other words, they still need to show that the chemical reaction works at the larger scale required to treat a human patient.

In a separate test, the team introduced the device to a large beaker filled with a sugary solution, to see if it could cope with larger volumes of glucose. The amount, about 1.3 gallons (5 liters), was similar to a person's total blood volume. The device still effectively controlled sugar levels in this larger system.

The test is not a substitute for research in larger animals and human patients, though, Fussenegger said. Those studies are the team's next priority.

Importantly, "our device is not intended to replace healthy nutrition, physical activity, or preventative medicine" for the treatment of diabetes and obesity, Fussenegger said.

"Obesity and type 2 diabetes are complex conditions involving much more than elevated glucose levels," he added. "We see it as a potentially powerful addition to the therapeutic toolbox, one that could eventually be combined with established treatments and lifestyle interventions."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Maity, D., Ray, P. G., Buchmann, P., Hamri, G. C., & Fussenegger, M. (2026). Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity. Science, 394(6822), eady8560. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ady8560

“What should I bring?” When a guest asks this well-intentioned question, the knee-jerk answer is “Wine!” But it’s just as simple to source thoughtful bits and bobs to create a memorable start to the meal. This way the host can forget about hors d’oeuvres altogether. Pick up a bark-wrapped cheese, artfully marbled charcuterie, or some I-can’t-believe-it’s-store-bought spritzes—or better yet, all of the above—and your fellow diners will be asking where they can buy a box on the way home.

If you are looking to contribute an NA option to the bar, you can’t do better than Ghia’s most recent release, Le Spritz Blood Orange. It’s a bubbly mix of bitter and sweet that more than fills in for an Aperol spritz or predinner glass of prosecco.

The problem with baked Brie is you have to bake it. Instead, bring a soft-rind cheese that can hold its own weight. Set it out on a plate or board for up to an hour before serving; this variety is best eaten at room temp when it’s soft and spreadable and the flavors have bloomed. St. Stephen from Four Fat Fowl in upstate New York is a triple-cream so buttery that even kids will go for seconds. Rush Creek Reserve is a dippable fondue-like wheel wrapped in spruce bark from Uplands in Dodgeville, WI.

#6571. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6569. Carne Guisada

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

With its warm spices and a rich gravy, this slow-braised carne guisada is perfect in tacos or on a bed of rice.

Carne guisada, a classic Mexican beef stew whose name translates to “stewed meat,” has a rich culinary backstory. Its roots stretch across northern Mexico and into Texas, where slow-braised beef dishes are a staple of home kitchens, taquerias and Tex-Mex restaurants alike. Tender beef simmers in a chili-based sauce, then is often served as a taco filling with soft flour tortillas. Some versions (especially in Texas) include potatoes to make it a one-pot meal. Others focus solely on the fall-apart meat and the smooth, peppery sauce built from dried chiles. You win either way.

For our carne guisada recipe, we keep the signature slow-cooked, deeply seasoned beef and rich gravy, but say yes to the potatoes for extra body and comfort. The use of beer, Worcestershire sauce and tomato paste brings layered depth that complements the traditional spices like cumin and chili powder. We aren’t claiming this is the only version because, honestly, that doesn’t exist. But this dish absolutely captures the spirit of classic carne guisada: tender meat, bold flavor and something meant to be shared.

In a large bowl, toss the beef with 1/4 teaspoon of salt. In a separate large bowl, combine the flour and paprika. Add the beef to the flour a few pieces at a time, tossing to coat them.

In a Dutch oven, heat the oil over medium heat. Brown the beef in batches, adding additional oil as necessary. Remove the pieces with a slotted spoon.

Editor’s Tip: Those browned bits stuck to the bottom of the pot are called fond, and they’re flavor gold. Don’t even think about washing them away.

To the same pan, add the onion. Cook and stir until it’s tender, three to five minutes. Stir in the tomato, jalapeno and garlic, and cook until they’re fragrant and the color starts to darken slightly.

Add the browned beef back to the pan. Add the beer, and bring it to a boil, scraping the bottom to release the browned bits. Simmer until the liquid is reduced by half, about five minutes.

Stir in the broth, Worcestershire sauce, crushed red pepper flakes, chili powder, cumin, bay leaf and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt, and bring the mixture to a boil. Reduce the heat, then cover the pot and simmer the stew until the meat is almost tender, about 1 hour and 30 minutes.

Add the potatoes and red wine vinegar. Cover the pot and simmer the stew until the meat and vegetables are tender, about 30 minutes longer.

Discard the bay leaf. Using the back of a spoon or ladle, slightly mash the potatoes. If desired, shred the beef slightly with two forks. Serve with tortillas, rice, lime and cilantro.

Let the carne guisada cool completely before transferring it to an airtight container. Store it in the refrigerator, where the flavors will actually deepen and improve overnight. It’s one of those dishes that might taste even better the next day. Carne guisada lasts up to four days in the refrigerator.

Carne guisada freezes very well. Store it in freezer-safe containers for up to three months, and thaw it overnight in the refrigerator before reheating.

Reheat carne guisada gently on the stovetop over medium-low heat until it’s warmed through. Add a splash of broth if the sauce has thickened too much.

You can use beef shoulder, bottom round or beef stew meat for carne guisada. The key is choosing a tougher cut with connective tissue that breaks down during the long, slow cooking time. This gives you that tender, fall-apart texture.

Whether you serve carne guisada on tortillas or rice, it also pairs beautifully with black beans, fresh salsa or even a side of warm cornbread.

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have observed a galaxy with a ring of newborn stars as it appeared 2.1 billion years after the Big Bang — hinting that the early universe may have been more chaotic than once thought.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A view of the possible ring galaxy GS18660 as seen by the James Webb Space Telescope. New observations hint that the ancient galaxy may have been created by a collision with an 'intruder' galaxy.

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have discovered a galaxy with a glowing ring of newborn stars shining in the early universe. The galaxy, which the researchers observed as it appeared just 2.1 billion years after the Big Bang, is the most distant ring galaxy ever found.

The ring galaxy, known as GS18660, may be the result of a collision between two galaxies, the researchers reported in their study, published Sept. 8 in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

It's rare to find the possible snapshot of a merger like this, given the timescales involved in these systems, Christopher Conselice, a professor of extragalactic astronomy at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science. Although interactions between galaxies may have been common in the early universe, the creation of ringed systems like this is thought to be unusual.

"In this sense, the galaxy system is quite unique and may give us important information about early galaxy formation," Conselice said in an email.

Scientists selected GS18660 for observation because it looked stretched out in older Hubble Space Telescope images.

"We therefore did not target GS18660 specifically as a ring galaxy," Michele Perna, a postdoctoral researcher at the Spanish Astrobiology Center and the first author of the study, told Live Science in an email. "When we observed it with JWST [Near-Infrared Spectrograph instrument], the much more detailed data revealed the prominent ring structure and allowed us to investigate the galaxy in three dimensions."

Using JWST, the team looked at the galaxy's unique shape, tracked the motions of its hot gas, analyzed the gas's chemical properties, and studied the galaxy's star formation history.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Another view of GS18660 as seen in an earlier Hubble Space Telescope survey.

When a small galaxy plunges through the center of a larger galaxy, the impact creates a wave of dense gas that ripples outward, similar to how water moves when a stone is dropped into a pond. As a result, a collisional galaxy is formed. Gas piles up along the wave and forms stars, producing a ring. These galaxies are rare in the local universe, and the few candidates found in the distant universe have been hard to confirm.

Several clues support the case for GS18660 as a collisional ring galaxy. For one, the researchers spotted a small companion galaxy, moving away from GS18660 at about 264 miles per second (425 kilometers per second). They also detected a bridge of gas linking the two, and the velocity along it changed, Perna noted. The change in velocity along this bridge-like structure indicates that the companion and GS18660 may be interacting.

Its position is also important, Perna added ‪—‬ the companion is located roughly along the main galaxy's minor axis, consistent with where an intruder would be expected to appear after a head-on plunge through the galaxy's disk.

Using the companion's speed and distance, the team estimated a rough timeline for the impact. It revealed that the collision happened about 17 million to 42 million years earlier in the galaxy's history. This time scale seems reasonable, Conselice said.

He explained that it is difficult to determine the age of a past interaction directly, but that if one did occur, it must have happened around the time a rapid star-formation episode began and its age should be consistent with the average ages of the star clusters.

Looking at star formation rates with different instruments, the team estimates that 10% to 20% of the stellar mass in the ring formed in the past few tens of millions of years. This suggests that the collision and the ring's burst of new stars might have happened at the same time, so they were most likely caused by the same event, Perna explained.

"It is not, by itself, definitive proof of a collision, but together with the bridge and the ring morphology, it strengthens the case for a recent impact," Perna noted.

The discovery may also shed light on how common these kinds of collisions used to be. Whereas earlier estimates suggested that collisional rings in the early universe might be about as rare as they are today ‪—‬ around 1 in 10,000 galaxies ‪—‬ the new findings hint that head-on collisions that form ring galaxies may be more common in the early universe.

"If GS18660 is confirmed as a collisional ring, it would therefore suggest that we need to revisit our estimates of how frequently these systems occur in the distant universe," Perna said

The team expressed caution about how much the data can prove. "It is really the combination of several pieces of evidence rather than one single observation," Perna said. "So we regard the collisional interpretation as our preferred scenario rather than a definitive conclusion."

Conselice thinks the evidence presented in the paper is consistent with a genuine collisional origin for the ring. "It looks to me like the merger hypothesis is more likely, given the nearby galaxy intruder and the stability of the intruder galaxy and the main galaxy itself," Conselice said. “Overall, it is convincing evidence that a past interaction and/or merger has occurred for this galaxy system based on the light distribution."

The other competing explanation involves a stellar bar. It proposes that the ring was not made by an intruder at all. GS18660 also shows a bar-like structure running north to south, and bars can funnel gas and stars into rings at specific distances from the center. Perna said the team cannot yet tell whether this is a true stellar bar or a result of the interaction.

A bar would be an exciting finding, too. JWST has already discovered barred galaxies in the early universe, including CEERS-2112. But researchers have not yet found a clear example of a bar-driven ring so early in the universe.

"Whether the ring was triggered by another galaxy or by the internal dynamics of GS18660," Perna said, "the result would tell us something important about how galaxies were already becoming structurally organised when the universe was only a few billion years old."Editor's note: This article was updated on Oct. 29 to correct a typo. In the image caption, the lead researcher's surname was mistakenly written as "Pera," rather than "Perna." This has been corrected.

#6564. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6559. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6558. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

A proposed shift in recommendations for hepatitis B vaccination in the U.S. could leave millions of young adults unprotected, a new modeling study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A proposed change to decades-old guidance on hepatitis B vaccination would lead to a dramatic increase in chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections among young people, a new modeling study predicts.

Previously, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended that all newborns be vaccinated against HBV within hours of birth ‪—‬ a strategy known as "universal birth-dose vaccination." But in December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) advised ending this recommendation, and the CDC accepted that advice.

The new guidance would recommend birth doses only to babies whose mothers tested positive for HBV or whose HBV status was unknown. The guidance suggests that mothers who test negative should instead ask their doctors about whether their child needs a birth dose — an approach the CDC calls "shared clinical decision-making." The new recommendation states that babies who forgo the birth dose should be at least 2 months old before starting the HBV vaccine series.

Health experts widely criticized the proposed change when it was announced, and for the moment, its implementation has been put on pause by legal action. The modeling study, published Oct. 19 in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, predicts what would happen if it came to pass.

"Overall, this modeling study has many strengths and I think presents an accurate projection of how the vaccine recommendations may impact future chronic HBV in the U.S.," Dr. Norah Terrault, a transplant hepatologist at the University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine who wasn't involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

When caught in infancy or early childhood, over 90% of HBV infections become chronic. About 15% to 25% of people with chronic HBV go on to develop liver scarring (cirrhosis), a form of liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma, or another chronic liver disease. So, an uptick in chronic HBV infections would translate to an uptick in these harmful liver conditions.

"Not every pregnant person is tested for hepatitis B," said study co-author Dr. Amir Mohareb, an infectious-diseases physician-investigator at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School. For those who are tested, there's a chance their results are inaccurate or that they're not provided the right care after testing positive. "Something can be missed at any step in the care process, so the vaccine dose at birth provides protection," he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Mohareb and his colleagues built a simulation model using published data, including the current prevalence of HBV and the screening rate among pregnant people. The team also factored in the HBV test's sensitivity, the share of children who are fully vaccinated by age 2, and the risk of developing chronic HBV infection in different age groups. They made estimates of how often children are exposed to the virus through contact with infected household or community members.

HBV is "very, very transmissible," Mohareb said. It can spread from mother to child at birth or through exposure to tiny amounts of bodily fluids, like blood from a scratch, after birth. So, even if a baby does not get HBV from their mother, if they are unvaccinated, they can still get from another family member or from other children.

Infants and young children have a greater risk of their HBV infections becoming chronic than people infected in adulthood.

With this data, the researchers tested what would happen if vaccination were postponed to 2 months of age for babies whose mothers tested negative. Among babies born in 2026, 19% more would have chronic HBV infections by age 20, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination, they found.

In this scenario, the babies would still start the HBV vaccine series, albeit two months later than usual. However, the CDC's proposed recommendation offers more wiggle room; it says that parents should consult with their children's doctors to "decide when or if their child will begin the hepatitis B vaccine series" at all.

The researchers ran a stimulation to compare these two scenarios: one where kids get their first shot two months late and one intended to capture this looser "shared clinical decision-making" scenario.

"Other vaccines whose recommendations employ similar language had uptake as low as 25%," Mohareb noted. This aspect of their modeling has some uncertainty, he emphasized, since it's unknown exactly how the public will respond to such loosening of the guidance.

The researchers assumed that about 87% of kids would complete the vaccine series by age 2 under the deferred strategy, while only 50% would under the shared decision-making strategy. That 50% coverage, in turn, would increase chronic HBV infections acquired by age 20 by 83%, and about 50% and 70% of those born under that guidance would be susceptible to HBV infection at age 20.

That's about 1.8 million people in this age group per year, compared with fewer than 250,000 under universal birth-dose vaccination. "This represents a population that is at risk for acquiring HBV via sex, drug use etc — behaviors more prevalent among young adults," Terrault said.

To test the robustness of the findings, Mohareb's team varied the most uncertain inputs across wide ranges and ran the model 1,000 times. In every simulation, the birth-dose strategy led to fewer chronic infections than either alternative.

These conclusions seem "robust" because "they are the same conclusions no matter how we change the numbers of the model," Mohereb noted. Though of course "the specific magnitude of change depends on how many people defer vaccination," he said.

The new study does not specifically show how many additional cases of liver disease or cancer would result from the uptick in HBV infections. But Terrault said that the risks of liver failure, cirrhosis and liver cancer "would be anticipated to increase due to the missed opportunity to protect against infection."

Mohareb stressed that he is in no way opposed to the principle of shared decision-making between doctors and patients. "They should always make the decision together," he said. "But we rely on our public health agencies not to tell us that we should be making decisions with the patient, but rather to tell us what policy would make us healthier as a country."

Childhood HBV infections in the U.S. dropped from more than 25,000 cases a year in 1985 to fewer than 100 reported cases in 2024. This steep decline is credited to HBV screening during pregnancy, antibody treatment for babies born to HBV-positive mothers and universal birth-dose vaccination.

"Certainly without following a universal dose vaccination recommendation there would be a lot more hep B infections early in life," Dr. Brian McMahon, a hepatologist and the director of the Liver Disease and Hepatitis Program at the Alaska Native Medical Center, told Live Science in an email.

Projected effect of 2026 federal changes to the childhood immunization schedule on chronic hepatitis B virus infections in the United States. #6554. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6553. Andy Cohen Reveals The Chaotic Meal He Enjoys With His Kids Every Sunday: 'This Is What Makes Us A Family'

Plus, the childhood snack combo he still swears by.

After enough New Year’s Eves throwing back shots with Anderson Cooper, Andy Cohen seems like someone you can trust on one very important topic: curing the dreaded next-day hangover.

“Gosh, just a cheeseburger,” Cohen tells me when I ask what food he swears by the morning after drinking. More specifically, he heads to Corner Bistro in New York City’s West Village for one.

Booze just so happens to be part of Cohen’s latest gig, as he’s teamed up with Svedka ahead of the 2027 Super Bowl.

After the brand’s AI Super Bowl ad drew heavy backlash last year, the vodka brand is challenging the public to create a commercial that’s even better. At stake is a $500,000 cash prize and the chance for the winning ad to air during the big game, with Cohen serving as one of the judges.

“I just think this contest is amazing, and I can’t wait to judge it,” he tells me. “This is really giving people a huge stage and permission to be creative surrounding a drink that I love.”

His taste in drinks may be his own, but burgers apparently run in the family—his son orders them during their weekly dinner ritual.

“We go out every Sunday night to the same restaurant in New York City, and [my daughter] has chicken noodle soup; he has a cheeseburger,” Cohen shares. “My daughter eats everything and has the best taste. She has pickles and broccoli with her soup—it’s the most disjointed meal. I have a turkey burger, but this is our process, and this is what makes us a family.”

Talking about what his kids eat also sent Cohen back to a few favorites from his own childhood. “Spaghettios and Doritos make a great combination,” he tells me, a pairing he grew up eating and still stands behind.

Then there’s Provel cheese, another longtime favorite. “[It’s a] big St. Louis thing; it’s kind of gross,” Cohen says.

Not exactly a ringing endorsement, but he still loves it anyway.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

#6550. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

Scientists sequenced the genome of a woman who lived 30,000 years ago and discovered that she had mixed Eastern and Western European ancestry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have sequenced the genomes of three Late Stone Age people who lived in Europe 30,000 years ago and discovered that they had closer biological ties than researchers previously thought. The new finding suggests that places like southwestern France may have been critical cultural hubs during the last ice age.

Shortly after Neanderthals disappeared from Europe, a Stone Age culture known as the Gravettian spread across the continent. Artifacts found during archaeological excavations ‪—‬ including portable art, such as "Venus figurines" ‪—‬ have shown that the Gravettian culture lasted from about 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. But ancient DNA has been recovered from only two dozen human skeletons from the Gravettian period, so questions about these people's ancestry remain unanswered.

Based on the small number of genomes from Gravettian people that were previously sequenced, experts believed that groups in Western Europe were largely separate from groups in Eastern Europe. But in a study published Oct. 23 in the journal Science Advances, researchers sequenced the genomes of three people who lived in what are now Spain, France and Italy during the Gravettian period. They discovered that one person had mixed genetic ancestry that revealed East-West exchange at least 30,000 years ago.

"Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," study first author Pere Gelabert, an evolutionary anthropologist at the University of Vienna, said in a statement.

The new information about mixed ancestry comes from a woman who died around 30,000 years ago and whose bones were found in Isturitz Cave in southwestern France. Originally used by Neanderthals, Isturitz Cave was occupied off and on from about 80,000 to 10,000 years ago. Cups made out of human skulls dated to roughly 15,000 to 12,000 years ago have also been found in Isturitz Cave.

Researchers found that the DNA from the Gravettian woman in Isturitz Cave was most similar to the previously known Western European genomes, but with an intriguing connection to Eastern and Central European groups.

This discovery of gene flow from the East is uncommon for the Late Stone Age, also known as the Upper Paleolithic, the researchers wrote in the study. It "could be explained by movements of people from Eastern Europe during the Gravettian period, which eventually contributed to this ancestry in Isturitz." Specifically, the researchers dated this "pulse" of gene flow to about 31,500 to 32,500 years ago.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The DNA evidence supports the archaeological theory that Isturitz Cave was an important cultural and biological hub for tens of thousands of years during the Late Stone Age, as the cave was located at a critical passage between continental Europe and the Iberian Peninsula, the researchers wrote.

All three newly sequenced Gravettian genomes revealed close biological connections to Western European groups, as well as genetic traits suggesting they had dark skin, dark hair and dark eyes. What's more, all of them had parents who weren't closely related to each other, suggesting that those populations may have actively avoided inbreeding.

"Overall, our results suggest that population structure and gene flow in western Europe during the Gravettian were more complex and dynamic than previously assumed," the researchers wrote.

Gelabert, P., Sawyer, S., Villalba-Mouco, V., Cheronet, O., Oberreiter, V., Gárate, D., Normand, C., Straus, L. G., González Morales, M. R., Gutiérrez-Zugasti, I., Cuenca-Solana, D., Darricau, J., de Lumley, H., Tejero, J.-M., Stahlschmidt, M., Higham, T., Giannì, M., van der Sluis, L. G., Gómez-Montes, C., … Pinhasi, R. (2026). Early Gravettian genomic data from Western Europe reveal population movements before the LGM. Science Advances, 12(43). https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh6128

#6546. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6545. Stuffed Pepper Soup

Stuffed peppers are one of the most versatile comfort foods. Literally—put anything in them, and they’ll taste great. The same goes for our stuffed pepper soup recipe. We take the classic stuffed pepper combination of ground beef, rice, tomatoes, and lots of cheese and turn those hearty flavors into an even more comforting soup that you can cozy up to all year long.

Grab a large pot and add in your favorite extra-virgin olive oil. Heat over medium heat, then add in your bell peppers and onion. Cook those down until soft while mixing occasionally—this should take around 7 minutes. Then, you can add the garlic and cook until fragrant, which should only take around 1 minute. Once everything is cooked down and fragrant, add the ground beef and season with salt and pepper. Season generously, but remember that you can always add more later; you can’t take it away. Once the beef is no longer pink, drain the fat and return the pot to the heat.

Once back on the heat, add the broth, crushed tomatoes, diced tomatoes, and your dried oregano. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer. Now it’s time to cook the rice. Add the rice and simmer while covered until the rice is tender. This should take around 40 minutes, but make sure to check on the rice every now and then. If you need a bit more liquid, add a little bit more water. Give it a taste, then season with salt and pepper as needed.

Once your soup is seasoned to your liking, garnish with shredded white cheddar (my personal favorite, but you do you) and some freshly chopped parsley for freshness.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Want to switch up this soup? Start by thinking about your favorite type of stuffed pepper. Do you like yours with ground turkey, ground pork, or sausage? What about using tomato paste for a richer flavor? Tomatillo sauce could replace tomato sauce. White beans, black beans, or navy beans might be the starchy addition if you prefer that over rice. If you’re vegan or vegetarian, fill your soup with zucchini, mushrooms, kale, or other favorite vegetables.

Stuffed pepper soup will last for no more than 3 to 4 days in the fridge. Make sure to seal tightly in a container if there are leftovers or you're meal prepping. The soup will last up to a month in the freezer. Let the soup thaw in the fridge before slowly reheating.
