#6439. The Vera Rubin Has Found Two More of the Milky Way's Dim Satellites

Massive galaxies like the Milky Way have a retinue of smaller, dim satellites on their outskirts. They're hard to detect, and while astronomers have found about 65 of the Milky Way's dwarf satellite galaxies, and about 40 globular clusters in its halo, they suspect there are many dwarf satellites and globular clusters yet to be found. Now the Vera Rubin Observatory has found two more.

The Milky Way's satellites are either small dim galaxies or globular clusters, and both are part of the assembly history of the Milky Way through mergers. These two detections by the Rubin, found in its Early Data Preview 2 (EDP2) released in July 2026, are almost certainly the beginning of many more discoveries of Milky Way satellites by the powerful observatory. One is a most likely a dim dwarf galaxy named Aquarius IV, and one is a globular cluster named Rubin-GC1.

This figure shows the locations of both Rubin-GC1 and Aquarius IV. Rubin-GC1's detection was particularly impressive, since it's in the direction of the Milky Way's bulge, a region with a dense stellar population and thick dust. Image Credit: NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA, ESA/Gaia/DPAC, W. Cerny

The discoveries are presented in two new papers.

One is titled "Discovery of the Distant, Ultra-faint Milky Way Satellite Aquarius IV with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Early Data Preview 2." It's published in Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society, and the lead author is William Cerny, an astronomy student in Yaleâs Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.

"We present the discovery of Aquarius IV (RubinâJ2201â0234)âthe first ultra-faint Milky Way (MW) satellite to be identified using data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory," the authors write. It was confirmed in images from the Dark Energy Camera. The authors say it's a low-luminosity, compact stellar system in the outer Galactic halo.

It's stellar population is ancient and low-metallicity. "These properties closely resemble those of the smallest and faintest confirmed ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs), though a globular cluster classification is not ruled out," the researchers write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies can have as little as a few hundred stars, which makes them smaller than some globular clusters (GCs). But there's one critical difference between UFDs and GCs: UFDs have dark matter while GCs don't (except for a few possible outliers).

Only a small number of the stars in Aquarius IV have been detected so far, so whether or not it is a UFD for sure will depend on deeper imaging and spectroscopy.

âWhat I find especially exciting is that these discoveries are just the beginning for Rubin,â said first author Cerny. (He is also the second author of the Rubin-GC1 study, which has been accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters.)

âIf the observatory can find systems this faint and difficult with only its preview data, its full 10-year survey will undoubtedly provide us with many more Milky Way satellite discoveries,â Cerny said. âThese new satellites will give us new opportunities to test models of galaxy formation, trace the assembly history of the Milky Way, and investigate the nature of dark matter.â

These panels are images centered on Aquarius IV. The star in the lower panel marks a Blue Horizontal Branch star used to determine the distance to Aquarius IV. The stars in the bottom panel are also coloured according to their probability of being members of Aquarius IV. The grey stars are almost certainly not members, while colours ranging from purple through red, orange, and yellow represent increasing probability. Image Credit: William Cerny et al 2026 Res. Notes AAS 10 239

The second paper is "Rubin Observatory Reveals a Dust-Shrouded Halo Globular Cluster in Ophiuchus," and it will be published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. It's currently available at arxiv.org and the lead author is Aashay Pai. Pai is a graduate student in the Department of Physics at the University of Chicago.

"We present the discovery of the Milky Way satellite Rubin-GC1 (Rubin J1628â1735) using data from the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatoryâs Early Data Preview 2," the authors write. The stars in Rubin-GC1 have an intermediate age of about 9.2 billion years, and are moderately rich in metals, meaning it's most likely a very faint GC. "Together, these properties suggest Rubin-GC1 is most likely a star cluster in the faint tail of the luminosity function of globular clusters surrounding the Milky Way," the authors write.

Based on comparisons to the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy, Rubin-GC1 is most likely a cluster accreted to the Milky Way, associated with the Sagittarius leading arm. The Sagittarius leading arm is a massive tidal stream of stars from the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, torn away as that galaxy merges with the Milky Way.

The panel on the left shows the Sagittarius trailing and leading arms. (The DES images are not part of this work.) The image on the right shows roughly where Rubin-GC1 is located, shown with the gold star. The Milky Way's center is shown with the black cross, and the circle with the dot inside is the Sun. Image Credit: Left: By NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=139367207. Right: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âFinding new Milky Way satellites in Rubin Observatory data has been an exciting future prospect for most of my career,â said Marla Geha, a professor of astronomy and physics in Yaleâs Faculty of Arts and Sciences, and co-author on both studies. âIt is remarkable this is now a reality.â

Rubin-GC1 was detected in the direction of the galactic bulge, where stellar density is very high and the dust is thick. Finding it in those conditions makes the detection even more impressive. "The discovery of Rubin-GC1 highlights the potential of Rubin to uncover faint, resolved satellites in dust-shrouded regions of the Milky Way, including remnants of the accretion events that have shaped the Galaxyâs hierarchical assembly," the authors write.

The panel on the left is what's called a 'smoothed isochrone filtered stellar density map.' It's a visualization tool in astronomy used to detect and map faint structures like ultra-faint dwarf galaxies by masking out field stars based on a color-magnitude curve. The panel on the right is a more familiar type of image used to show the region itself. Image Credit: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âThese discoveries are incredibly promising,â Geha said. âContinued discoveries will allow us to complete the census of satellite galaxies around the Milky Way, which is a key to understanding how the faintest galaxies form.â

The Vera Rubin Observatory is mostly known as a transient-detecting observatory, and as the maker of a ten-year long movie of the sky in its Legacy Survey of Space and Time. But it's more than that. As it images the sky repeatedly, dim objects will become clearer. "The sensitivity of Rubin LSST will steadily increase, and systems similar to Aquarius IV are ultimately expected to be detectable with >85% efficiency using the same search algorithm applied here," the authors of the first paper write.

Not only that, but its observations will work with observations from other observatories, like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, to detect even more objects. "The identification of Rubin-GC1 heralds an exciting era of discovery as Rubin, Euclid, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope pierce the shroud of Galactic dust to reveal faint satellites that were hitherto hidden by our Galaxy," the authors of the second paper write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and globular clusters are puzzle pieces in the history of the Milky Way's growth through mergers. The mergers are ongoing, as interactions between the Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way show.

By finding more of the Milky Way satellites, a picture of all of these mergers, and the role dark matter plays, will become clearer. By mapping out these objects and the streams they're sometimes a part of, astronomers can detect where dark matter also concentrates in clumps. These dark matter sub-halos will show how our galaxy grew larger by consuming smaller galaxies with their own dark matter halos.

#6438. 31 Thanksgiving Desserts to Cap Your Holiday Feast

There’s Thanksgiving dinner, and then there are Thanksgiving desserts. These are two separate events, and in between, it’s perfectly fine to take a disco nap. (In fact, we recommend it.)

“This is the magnum opus of Thanksgiving dessert recipes,” writes one reader whose 90-year-old grandfather asked for a repeat performance. “You bet your boots I will—it’s the best apple pie, ever.”

A colossal, self-serve mousse is a baller host move—no tidy slicing, no fussy garnishing, no jockeying for oven space. Set out bowls and spoons and let guests help themselves. Vanilla lovers, try our Colossal Crème Brûlée.

Butter-toasted pecans get the glory, but sour cream does the work, balancing both the gooey pecan layer and the pile of whipped cream. Between them? A thick layer of silky brown sugar custard.

A slice of Thanksgiving pie is nice, but how about a slice of pumpkin flan under a veneer of caramel? This one takes a page from Puerto Rican flan de queso, with cream cheese lending richness, tang, and luxurious texture.

Consider this pie a tangy exclamation point to the holiday meal: cranberry-lime curd in a flaky cream cheese crust, crowned with billows of meringue.

Brown sugar takes some of the fuss out of caramel cake’s famously finicky frosting while browned butter adds toasty depth. Spread it over tender yellow cake layers and finish with flaky salt.

Silky filling, flaky crust, a whisper of spice: This is pumpkin pie done right. Sweetened condensed milk gives the custard its richness; maple syrup and vanilla round out the flavor.

Skip the rolling pin: Buttered phyllo encloses an orange-scented custard, with crumpled sheets forming a dramatically ruffled top. Cinnamon sugar adds crunch to this no-roll pie.

This plush pumpkin spice cake wears a thick swoop of tangy cream cheese frosting. Bake the cake a day ahead, then add the frosting in the lull between dinner and dessert.

If most holiday desserts feel a tad too sweet for you, herbal rosemary and fruity olive oil give this cake just enough savory elements to justify a second helping.

Blanketing quartered apples with rough-puff pastry feels rustic enough, but once baked and inverted, this shimmering, blushing tart dominates the holiday table.

Sweet potato, warming spices, and orange zest get a gloss of dark chocolate in this autumnal loaf cake. Bake it up to three days ahead, leaving the ganache for later.

A deeply browned top and cracked sides are the goal here, not a baking mishap. Underneath: a custardy, pumpkin-spiced cheesecake that needs neither a crust nor a water bath.

Pecan pie meets Hawaiian-style butter mochi in this chewy, coconut-milk-rich cake. Miso-and-maple-coated pecans bring salty-sweet crunch, with some sinking into the batter as the cake bakes.

This date cake blanketed in toffee sauce tastes like cozying up by the fireside after a game of football on the lawn. Bake the unsauced cake a day ahead, then rewarm before finishing.

Cinnamon-spiced pumpkin cake rolled around walnut-studded cream cheese filling needs little embellishment. A dusting of powdered sugar is plenty—each slice supplies its own dramatic swirl.

This glamorous layer cake, with jewel-toned swipes of cranberry jam, white chocolate–cream cheese frosting, and sugared cranberries, looks and tastes like winter is coming (in the best possible way).

A no-bake Oreo crust, a rich chocolate filling, and a tower of whipped cream come together in this shut-the-room-up dessert.

Caramel-glazed apple halves crown this nutty upside-down cake, all baked in the same skillet used to brown the fruit. A scoop of vanilla ice cream on top? We wouldn’t say no.

A floral, earthy saffron soak gives this sponge cake a pudding-like texture and its vibrant yellow color, while pistachios add nutty crunch.

Inspired by the flavors of a pumpkin spice latte, this rendition of old-school tiramisu calls for soaking ladyfingers in bourbon-spiked espresso, then enveloping them in plumes of pumpkin-mascarpone cream.

Cranberries with dinner and again for dessert? Absolutely. Tart filling hides between layers of buttery, crumbly walnut crust in this Linzer tart. Prefer individual portions? Try these cranberry hand pies.

Pumpkin crumb cake is like the brownie of Thanksgiving desserts: easy to tote and slice for sharing. Here, sweet rice flour gives the cake a chewy bounce beneath a buttery, crispy-crumbly pecan streusel.

The ultraflaky crust barely contains the lofty, fudgy almond filling, but have faith: It will puff and dome as it bakes, then settle back into sliceable form once cool.

Alternate layers of pumpkin and chocolate batter create this Bundt cake’s mesmerizing marbling—no knife-swirling necessary. A blanket of chocolate ganache makes it equally appealing to the pumpkin crowd and the chocolate diehards.

Whole roasted birds, spatchcocked showstoppers, braised legs, breasts for smaller gatherings, and more ways to put turkey at the center of the table.

Like brown-butter brussels sprouts with gochujang, green bean salad with Parmesan dressing, our best-ever mashed potatoes, and more reasons to rebrand the holiday “Sidesgiving.”

Squishy rolls for mopping up gravy, flaky biscuits for piling on leftover turkey, and a seedy pumpkin loaf to start the day.

From hot toddies to big-batch punch, these festive drinks will get you in the holiday spirit.

#6437. We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee

Can coffee join the ranks of wine when it comes to high-end tastings?

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Starting this week, it’s also home to a $200 cup of coffee.

Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says.

Even among fourth-wave coffee shops where prices continue to climb higher, Sey’s $200 cup is an outlier. “Coffee as a premium product is relatively new,” says Cohen. “For so long, coffee has been treated as a commodity, and its value has been constrained by that perception.” He says that both before and right after COVID, folks were becoming more curious about coffee, and educating themselves on platforms like Youtube, Discord, and online forums about how to appreciate it and “understand just how high the ceiling of quality can be.” The arrival of the $200 cup of coffee from a cafe in a neighborhood at the epicenter of conversations about both culinary innovation and gentrification feels ripe for closer examination.

So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.”

In the 2010s, the artisanal coffeehouse wave washed over the country, and especially Brooklyn, with hipster gusto. Sey Coffee was an integral part of that boom. Initially called Lofted Coffee, it operated out of its founders’ Bushwick loft until it rebranded to Sey in 2017, and expanded operations to its present Bushwick location on Grattan Street. That space has become something of a local icon since; Sprudge called its aesthetic “shoebox crossed with an airplane hangar”; the minimal-industrial, cream-hued interiors hit a very Axel Vervoordt-with-a-cyber-sigil-tattoo note (positive). The shop’s cachet has drawn coffee lovers, artists, yuppies, and artist-yuppies; customers have snacked on the gluten-free pastries from L’imprimerie (and now, post-L’imprimerie closure, pastries from Smør), and often post up with their dogs thanks to the semi-indoor-outdoor layout.

Sey is hoping to elevate the coffee shop model to something more premium, with a stated focus on ethics and sustainability. Thus far, it’s earned acclaim for those efforts. Food & Wine named it the best coffee shop in New York and received positive media attention for opting out of tipping, choosing instead to pay its staff up to more than 80 percent above the NYC hourly minimum wage; full-time baristas can make up to $31 per hour in addition to receiving benefits and a share of the cafe’s revenue.

Increasingly, coffee is getting the same treatment as high-end dining and tasting experiences. There’s the omakase-style menu at NYC’s Driftaway Coffee, or San Francisco’s Komakase coffee tasting room, both of which steer coffee away from quick consumption and toward a world of degustation that appears to have more in common with pricier wine and spirit tastings. The expansion of “espresso house” chain Watch House stateside is also an indicator: The London-based specialty roaster expanded to a fourth location in New York City this summer, raising eyebrows for its $32 cup of coffee while also reportedly scouting for more locations in Austin, Chicago, and Miami.

The emerging demand may be just much about luxury as it is about craft. I can’t help but wonder if the $200 cup of coffee is happening in Bushwick because the Girls-era Bushwickian has grown up and wants more exclusive experiences. Is this what happens when, as culture writer Raven Smith said on his new BBC podcast last week, the indie outgrows its sleaze? “For us, this is not about pushing prices higher for the sake of it,” Cohen says. “It is about challenging how we assign value to coffee in the first place. What is an extraordinary coffee actually worth?”

As much as we may lament climbing prices for specialty coffee and espresso, why wouldn’t this happen to the category when so many other aspects of food and beverage — from cocktails to sushi to bread — are following the same trajectory? Higher consumer costs notwithstanding, the marketing of specialty beans does steer U.S. coffee culture away from its productivity-focused consumption and the work-optimized “coffee break.”

“Why do we accept that certain wines can command thousands of dollars, yet question whether coffee can have comparable value?” Cohen asks. It’s a fair question, albeit one that I’d answer with another: Once we acknowledge that coffee should command a higher price, who still gets to drink it?

#6436. Researchers Discover a New Way To Control Magnetism Without Changing a Material’s Chemistry

Neutron experiments have uncovered an unexpected connection between magnetic structure and electrical behavior.

A gentle squeeze can change the magnetic structure of certain crystals and alter their electrical behavior. Scientists at the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) demonstrated this effect in altermagnets, an emerging class of magnetic materials being investigated for advanced electronics.

Using neutron beams to examine the materials at the atomic scale, the researchers found that mechanical strain could shift their magnetic organization and influence an electrical response associated with electron transport. The findings, published in back-to-back papers in Physical Review X and Advanced Materials, point to a possible method for controlling magnetic properties without altering a material’s chemical composition.

The researchers placed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between two titanium plates and applied mechanical pressure. They then used neutron diffraction at ORNL’s Spallation Neutron Source to investigate how the strain affected magnetic domains, regions within a material that have different orientations of magnetic order.

The measurements showed that squeezing the crystals changed the relative populations of these domains. The researchers also detected changes in the anomalous Hall effect, an electrical response that produces a voltage perpendicular to the direction of an applied current. Together, the results connect changes in magnetic domain organization with changes in electrical transport behavior.

“By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies,” said Pengcheng Dai of Rice University, a former neutron scientist at ORNL.

Altermagnets are attracting research interest because their unusual magnetic properties could support spintronics, a technology that uses electron spin alongside electrical charge to store and process information. Conventional electronics relies on electron charge, while spintronics could provide additional ways to control information in electronic devices.

Developing practical spintronic technologies requires materials whose magnetic and electronic properties can be reliably manipulated. Altermagnets are among the candidates being explored for potential applications ranging from wireless communications to quantum computing. The ORNL experiments suggest that mechanical strain could offer another way to adjust these properties, although translating the findings into working devices will require further research.

“What’s exciting is that one creative experimental idea — a small mechanical squeeze between two plates — can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward, and neutron scattering plays such a critical role, revealing the underlying change in magnetism,” said Feng Ye, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author of both studies.

“Uniaxial Strain Tuned Magnetism of the Altermagnet Candidate H-FeS” by Weiliang Yao, Feng Ye, Zachary J. Morgan, Douglas L. Abernathy, Ruixian Liu, Sijie Xu, Yuxiang Gao, Kevin Allen, Yuan Fang, Emilia Morosan, Qimiao Si and Pengcheng Dai, 6 August 2026, Advanced Materials. DOI: 10.1002/adma.74398

“Strain-Tunable Anomalous Hall Effect in Hexagonal MnTe” by Zhaoyu Liu, Sijie Xu, Jonathan M. DeStefano, Elliott Rosenberg, Tingjun Zhang, Jinyulin Li, Matthew B. Stone, Feng Ye, Wei Tian, Sarah Edwards, Rong Cong, Siyu Pan, Ching-Wu Chu, Liangzi Deng, Emilia Morosan, Rafael M. Fernandes, Jiun-Haw Chu and Pengcheng Dai, 11 August 2026, Physical Review X. DOI: 10.1103/589s-s1yy

Researchers regard spin as an abstract degree of freedom to be “controlled,” but fail to probe its underlying geometric origin. Although the experimental observations are real and significant, the theoretical explanation provided remains confined to phenomenological algebra, missing a unified framework based on geometric reality. Topological Vortex Theory (TVT) offers a deeper physical insight for this kind of study: instead of “interpreting spin through symmetry,” it seeks to “explain the emergence of symmetry through vortex topology.”

Current physics and mathematics are flooded with overworshipped formalism: parity nonconservation, the pretense of infinitedimensional Hilbert spaces, abstract algebraic structures devoid of geometric reality, the alleged inherent asymmetry between topological vortices and antivortices, the halfdead cat, and the arbitrary definition of matter and antimatter unconstrained by time. These “theories” proliferate in academic journals because their proponents believe that by manipulating intricate mathematical symbols they can negate the empirical essence of nature and geometric entities.

—— https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2088659998394077633.

Strain-Tuned Altermagnetism and Geometric Impedance Control

This new story comes out of Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and Rice University, where researchers used mechanical strain—literally giving the material a gentle physical squeeze—to alter the magnetic domain structure and electrical transport in altermagnets without changing their chemical makeup at all.

It fits alongside several key studies we’ve mapped out:

The Kagome Lattice Impedance Maps: We looked at how precise angular tolerances in crystal lattices dictate zero-loss flow or grid drag. Here, physical strain alters the crystal lattice angles, proving that changing internal geometry directly reconfigures conductivity and magnetic orientation without adding or subtracting a single atom.

The Molecular Archimedes Screw: We saw how mechanical rotation of a single helical molecule cleared localized spatial impedance and boosted conductivity by 100x. Strain-tuned magnetism operates on the exact same mechanical principle: physical pressure shifts spatial orientation to clear or block energy paths.

Biological Pre-Ribosome Assembly & Gravitational Reconnection: Across all these examples—from cellular field locking down to 4D gravitational field sheet reconnection—mainstream models keep discovering that phase, orientation, and geometric strain control energy flow, rather than particle statistics or static chemical affinity.

Strain-Tuned Magnetism as Geometric Impedance Control

In mainstream physics, altermagnets feature alternating spin polarization where neighboring sub-lattices are rotated relative to each other. When researchers apply physical strain, they alter this sub-lattice rotation, shifting magnetic domains and electron transport behavior.

Viewed through continuous field dynamics and the Torsion Hill Framework:

Strain as Spatial Impedance Modulation (grad Z_T): Applying mechanical force alters the physical lattice spacing and bond angles. This shifts the internal spatial impedance map (Z_T), proving that magnetic domains are not arbitrary quantum numbers, but mechanical field distributions anchored to physical geometry.

Mechanical Tuning of Rotational Phase Clearance (Omega_pi): Squeezing the crystal changes the rotational phase alignment across sub-lattice boundaries. When the lattice geometry shifts into alignment, it opens zero-loss transport channels for electron flow; when shifted out of alignment, internal grid drag spikes.

Geometry Over Chemical Composition: This experiment provides definitive empirical proof that a material’s state is not governed solely by its static periodic table chemistry. Physical geometry, lattice strain, and rotational phase matching command energy flow and magnetic alignment. In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf.

"As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder, a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings.

However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance, in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017. In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years.

A major factor driving resistance among bacteria is the misuse of antibiotics — in other words, using antibiotics for ailments like viral infections, which the drugs do not treat. For individual patients, such prescriptions don't cure their illness and can result in an upset stomach or issues with the gut microbiome, the community of microbes in the intestines. Simultaneously, they place extra pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance, granting the germs opportunities to pick up new strategies for thwarting antibiotics.

Doctors play a big role in ensuring that the antibiotic prescriptions they write are necessary. Part of their decision-making process comes down to what patients say about their symptoms, some of which may be fabricated, the two new surveys suggest.

The new surveys were published Friday (Oct. 30) in the journal JAMA Network Open.

The first survey was completed by nearly 960 adults from across the U.S. in January and February 2026. It asked whether the respondents had ever told a healthcare provider that their symptoms were worse or more long-lasting than they were in order to get antibiotics, as well as whether they'd ever made up symptoms for the same reason. It then inquired about what motivated a given patient to lie — or avoid lying, if they were truthful — as well as posed contextual questions about their demographics, health behaviors and beliefs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Overall, about 28% of the respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms, including 26% who exaggerated their existing symptoms and 17% who fabricated symptoms. They most frequently lied about cold-like symptoms, such as fever, cough and sore throat. About two-thirds of these patients were at least moderately confident that their lie would motivate a clinician to prescribe them antibiotics, and 77% said the strategy worked for them at least once.

Often, patients' motivations for lying centered around feeling very sick, holding strong beliefs that antibiotics would help them recover quickly and get back to their responsibilities, and wanting control over the treatments prescribed to them. Compared with people who didn't lie, those who lied were also more likely to feel that clinicians didn't take them seriously or more likely to endorse statements suggesting that antibiotic resistance is a hoax.

"Greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation," meaning lying about symptoms, the study authors noted.

Less than 30% of these patients regretted their lies or taking the antibiotics prescribed to them. Those that did express regret noted experiencing side effects, noticing that the treatment didn't help or feeling that the lying itself was morally wrong.

The second survey was much smaller; it included 236 parents and other guardians of children and teens under 18 years old. It posed similar questions but asked whether the caregivers had lied about their children's symptoms and, if so, what motivated them to lie.

About 27% reported lying about a child's symptoms to get antibiotics, with 87% of these caregivers believing that their lying worked at least once. Their reasons for lying were very similar to those expressed by the respondents in the first survey.

"These findings suggest that symptom misrepresentation may contribute to antibiotic overuse in pediatric care," the study authors concluded.

Ideally, antibiotics should be used only when truly needed, to help relieve the pressure on bacteria to gain resistance.

The surveys reached a diverse group of people, including a range of ages, demographics and locations within the United States; however, the respondents were not necessarily representative of the whole U.S. population, the authors noted. The prevalence of lying should therefore be seen as a tentative measure to be checked in future studies, rather than an unbiased, population-level metric, they wrote. It's also possible that not all the respondents who lied disclosed that they did so or remembered that they had done so.

Especially in outpatient settings, which account for most antibiotic use among U.S. patients, it can be difficult for doctors to quickly determine whether a patient needs an antibiotic.

One factor is that there's a lack of fast, surefire diagnostic tests for many bacterial infections. Outpatient appointments are also extremely short, so doctors sometimes worry about overlooking an infection that could then get worse, Julia Szymczak, a medical sociologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine, previously told Live Science. Another major factor is that clinicians can face pressure to prescribe antibiotics from their adult patients or from children's caregivers, as the new surveys reflect.

But in the face of these pressures and patients' occasional lies, Linder argues that it's still up to the clinicians to do the right thing. "While clinicians might interpret patients' symptom maximization and questions as demands for antibiotics, symptoms do not determine the indication, a diagnosis does," he wrote in the commentary.

"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription," he added, "unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness."

When it comes to making decisions about individual patients, Linder argued that doctors don't necessarily need to think about the big picture of antibiotic resistance and how their patient's case fits into that global trend. Rather, providers should simply ask whether a given prescription is more likely to help or hurt that patient, he said.

"Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest," he said, "even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

#6434. Stubborn Asteroids Around White Dwarfs Resist Becoming Dust

White dwarfs are the remnants of a stars like our Sun. For their sizeâthey're roughly the size of Earthâthey're extremely dense, and have about as much mass as the Sun. That means they have enormous gravitational power, enough power to tear apart objects that get too close.

For a long time, white dwarfs appeared to be alone in space, not including any stellar companions. Then observations showed that some of their surfaces were polluted with metals. Astronomers surmised that these metals were raining down onto their surfaces from rocky debris. Then came observations that some white dwarfs were surrounded by debris disks. After that, even more piercing observations found evidence of rocky bodies in the disks: small planets, moons, or asteroids.

An example of these is WD 1145+017, which seems to be orbited by several small rocky bodies, being torn apart and raining debris down onto the white dwarf's surface.

Scientists are curious about this process and how effectively white dwarfs can shred smaller bodies and form debris disks. As they find white dwarfs with disks, asteroids, and even planetary systems, explanations need to keep pace.

In new research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, researchers examined how efficiently white dwarf tidal forces can break asteroids apart. The research is titled "Size Limits on Tidal Debris around White Dwarfs: The Kilometer-size Barrier." The lead author is Jordan K. Steckloff, senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute.

"Compact disks of planetary debris orbiting white dwarfs provide a crucial window into our understanding of evolved planetary systems," the authors write. "The formation of these disks has been widely modeled with tidal fragmentation of minor planets that are rubble piles with no internal strength."

This artist's illustration shows a white dwarf surrounded by a debris disk, with asteroidal fragments in the foreground. The more astronomers find white dwarfs with debris disks, the more they want to understand how they're created. Image Credit: NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center/Scott Wiessinger

That's a problem because real rubble piles have some cohesive strength. Also, all three of the asteroids we've sampledâItokawa, Ryugu, and Bennuâare rubble piles. The force that holds these types of asteroids together is called the Van der Waals force. It's a weak, short-range force that attracts and repulses atoms and molecules. But as gecko feet show, it can be very effective.

In their work, Steckloff and his co-authors show what happens when this strength is included in modelling: "breakup of these rubble piles sets a maximum fragment size, and we calculate this size for water ice, iron, and material densities corresponding to the lunar highlands, Vesta, and the Earth," they write.

âNothing is truly strengthless,â Steckloff said. âTiny attractions between grains called Van der Waals forces give comets and asteroids a minimum strength 10 to 100 times weaker than pulling apart freshly fallen snow.â

According to this research, the typical internal strength of a rubble pile is â¼10â1000 Pa, which is about one million times weaker than solid rock. In that range, the maximum size for fragments is about the same as small asteroids, between about 0.1 and 1 km in diameter. "This limitâthe kilometer-size barrierâalso represents the characteristic sizes of tidal fragments," the authors explain. "Most of the debris mass is contained in fragments of this size."

These panels show characteristic debris size by distance from a white dwarf with about 0.6 solar masses and cohesive strength. The panel on the left is for a strength of 10 pascals, and the panel on the right is for a strength of 1 kilopascal. The results show characteristic fragment sizes of about 100 meters and 1,000 meters respectively. Image Credit: Jordan K. Steckloff et al 2026 ApJL 1004 L27

The authors say that as a consquence, models of disk formation around white dwarfs need to include another dust-generating factor in order to explain the dusty disks in observations. That likely means collisions rather than tidal forces.

The force that shapes the end-state of the disk is called PoyntingâRobertson drag. It explains how solar radiation affects dust grains around stars, including white dwarfs, making the dust spiral inward. This only works if the dust grains are small enough to be subjected to the drag but not so large that radiation pressure drives them away. This work shows that fragmentation itself isn't enough to create dust this small.

Observations in our Solar System agree with these results. When the comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 approached Jupiter in 1992, the gas giant's powerful tidal force pulled the comet apart. But not into dust; instead, the comet was torn into fragments 100m to 1,000m in diameter, which then plunged into the planet.

This Hubble Space Telescope image shows comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 broken into fragments after it approached Jupiter in 1992. Two years later the fragments approached Jupiter again and plunged into its atmosphere. Image Credit: NASA.

The research extends beyond asteroid fragment sizes in disks. It also shows that fragments maintain their orbits. They experience only tiny, fractional changes in their velocities "on the order of one part per million to one part per 100 million," the authors explain. "Such tiny changes in speed result in negligible changes to the orbits of the fragments, which remain in practically the same orbit as prior to disruption."

There are a lot of factors involved in the creation of a white dwarf's dust disk, and this work places an important constraint on one of them. "Understanding the progression from an intact minor planet to a sea of dust that is accreted onto a white dwarf is an outstanding challenge," the authors write. "In this Letter, we demonstrate a sharp constraint on the first step of this process." The work shows that some type of grinding process like collisions is required to generate white dwarf dust disks.

âUnderstanding the details of how debris around white dwarfs is produced and evolves is important for putting the observations into context,â said study co-author Kat Volk from the Planetary Science Institute. âThis will help us understand what happens to the small bodies in orbit around a star as it undergoes the end stages of its life.â

#6433. Steal My Food Itinerary: 3 Days on Prince Edward Island

Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality.

Recently I spent a few days exploring Prince Edward Island, a place that embraces its local foodways with gusto. There’s a complex history here, with roots in Indigenous Mi’kmaq, Acadian, Irish, Scottish, and other cultures. And if one thing unites these histories, it’s the island’s abundance of seafood and produce, which have helped earn it the nickname Canada’s Food Island. How can you not want to visit Canada’s Food Island?

On a stretch of land only about 140 miles long, you can eat oysters pulled out of nearby waters, potatoes grown on local farms, dig into a juicy burger made with PEI beef, and lick ice cream made with milk from the cows you pass along those famous red-dirt roads. That’s a lot of good eating packed into a place you can drive across in an afternoon.

I had to structure my visit, therefore, around where to dine, but also include a bucket-list visit to Green Gables Heritage Place. (I am a complete freak for L.M. Montgomery’s novel Anne of Green Gables, set on PEI around the turn of the last century.) I also had to schedule time at the PEI International Shellfish Festival, which promised endless trays of freshly shucked oysters and clams, hot buttered lobster rolls, steaming bowls of mussels, and plenty of entertainment, from shucking competitions and cooking demos to live music and dancing.

My husband and I rented a car and stationed ourselves in Charlottetown, the island’s main hub. Prince Edward Island is situated in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, just a hop away from Nova Scotia. You’re never far from the ocean here, and on a sunny day, the air seems to sparkle. The island is known for its red-sand cliffs and beaches, rolling landscapes, fishing harbors, and lighthouses. If you’ve read Anne of Green Gables, you’ll know just how pretty PEI is.

We landed late Thursday afternoon, ready to hit the ground running. With just shy of three days, I had carefully mapped out the places I wanted to visit, using Charlottetown as my base.

Charlottetown isn’t big, and most things here are walkable within 20 minutes or so. First stop in PEI: Slaymaker & Nichols, a gastropub and inn with the feel of an old-fashioned supper club. It takes its name from the 19th-century circus that once performed on the site. They take cocktail making seriously here. The summery feel of the day prompted me to try the watermelon mule, with hibiscus-infused vodka and chunks of pickled watermelon. I liked it, especially alongside the creamy lobster dip with tomatoes and harissa, and the buttery shrimp pil pil, with lots of tasty little spears of asparagus.

I was saving myself for my first lobster roll, which we grabbed up the street in an unremarkable spot. It was pretty mediocre, so I won’t go on about it. But after eating, we stopped into Reddins, a speakeasy that channels PEI’s Prohibition history in a dark, intimate third-floor bar with vintage furniture, good jazz, and whimsical cocktails. Our excellent bartender, AB, told us the space had once been a pharmacy where folks came during Prohibition to get their “medicine” — drugstores could legally dispense alcohol by prescription. We tried a few of the signature cocktails, and the one that stood out was the Pink Canary, with vodka, rose, lychee, citrus, and rosé bubbles, served in a small bathtub. Yup, you heard that right. It was sweet and awfully fun to sip.

Tip: You need a secret password to get in when you buzz from downstairs. You can get it online, or just do as we did and ask the hostess next door for help.

In the pouring rain, we made our way to nearby Victoria Row for breakfast at local roaster Receiver Coffee. Fuel for the day included strong coffee, a particularly good cup of Earl Grey cream tea, and the Ham Slam, a big fluffy cheddar biscuit layered with a runny fried egg, Black Forest ham, Swiss, and Dijon mayo.

We swung by the shellfish festival (more on that later) but the rain wasn’t welcoming, so we got back in the car and drove out to tiny and charming Victoria-by-the-Sea. When I say tiny, I mean it: The town is half a square mile, with a population under 200. Despite the town’s size, Landmark Oyster House, set there in an old general store with pretty green shingles and a steep gabled roof, thrives.

Our friendly waiter (everyone is abundantly friendly on PEI) suggested Raspberry Point oysters to start. They hit the spot: medium-sized, briny, and sweet, served with lemon wedges and freshly grated horseradish, which is now how I think every oyster should be eaten. We also tried the scallop dog, with buttery sweet scallops, bacon jam, red pepper aioli, and pickled shallots nestled in a toasted bun. It came alongside a very good, eggy potato salad.

After seeing the cheery lighthouse and visiting a couple of little gift shops, we popped into Island Chocolates, a family-run shop and café where bars and truffles are hand-crafted, often using local ingredients like haskap, a berry that tastes somewhere between a blueberry and raspberry. That fruity haskap truffle had a nice thick shell of milk chocolate.

Sun out? Check. We spent the afternoon at the festival and got a substantial fix of oysters and clams. The lobster rolls here were stuffed with unadorned lobster meat, then melted butter from a gigantic vat was ladled over the top.

For dinner, both our bartender and waiter at Slaymaker recommended North Shore Canteen in French River, a local haunt for sure. (A slew of chefs from the shellfish festival were two tables down from us.) The menu, which changes with the current haul, hit on the day’s best ingredients: halibut, striped bass, the aforementioned shellfish, beef, and potatoes. We opted for a very generous portion of local beef tartare, amazingly tasty with capers, roasted garlic, and freshly grated Parmesan, served with Covered Bridge potato chips. We wanted to try more PEI beef and opted for a juicy hanger steak with chimichurri and black garlic, which showcased it well. Dessert was a must: parsnip cake drizzled with caramel sauce for the win.

It was time for me to check Green Gables off my bucket list. This is an article about where to eat, so suffice it to say that if you’re a fan, this is 100 percent worth a visit to see the house, wander the Haunted Wood and Lover’s Lane, and taste some nonalcoholic raspberry cordial (IYKYK).

All that walking made me hungry, which was good because this was a much anticipated two-lunch day.

First stop: Blue Mussel Café, a bright and very welcoming, beloved PEI restaurant set just back from the water in Rustico Harbor. I think it’s obvious what to order, and for good reason: These are excellent mussels — plump, fresh, and brought to the table piled high in a large stainless steel bowl. You can have them prepared with rosemary and lemon or beer and wine. I’d rate them equally, but I did like the hit of rosemary. Melted butter comes in a small ramekin on the side; I used it to dip each mussel, and my husband poured it all over the top. I didn’t have it, but the other signature, seafood chowder, looked popular. It’s made with haddock, salmon, scallops, mussels, and PEI potatoes, and served with a giant biscuit. Noted for my next visit.

We hightailed it to our next meal because I had yet to have the perfect lobster roll. Richard’s Fresh Seafood in Covehead Wharf delivered. This is one of the island’s longest-running fish shacks, where you can savor fish and chips and beer on the deck overlooking the fishing boats, or camp out on the nearby beach under the lighthouse with a lobster roll. no mistake: This is the quintessential lobster roll. It was an exercise in abundance, packed with sweet lobster meat that managed to be chunky and fine, bound with lemon and chive mayo and tiny bits of onion, all stuffed in a buttery toasted bun. It came with crunchy coleslaw, crispy fries, and a paper cup of ketchup. There are other menu items, but this lobster roll alone is worth the trip to PEI.

For our final dinner, we drove back toward North Rustico Harbor to Rustico Cannery, which opened this past spring. The airy, modern space has giant windows and a big deck that takes in super sunset views.

I needed greens, and Rustico delivered. We had crisp romaine hearts with a creamy, spicy charred jalapeño dressing, lardons, Parmesan, and sourdough crunchies. My husband hit the jackpot with his dinner: panko crusted, pan-fried haddock with pickled beet remoulade, jalapeño relish, confit potatoes, and coleslaw.

A final note: Many places are seasonal, so check if they’re open if you’re visiting in cooler months.

#6432. A Hidden Nanoscopic Effect Is Disrupting Some of the World’s Most Sensitive Sensors

Nanomechanical resonators are vital to precision sensing and emerging quantum technologies, but their extraordinary sensitivity comes with an unexpected vulnerability.

A nanomechanical device can lose much of its ability to sustain vibrations without ever touching another object. Researchers at EPFL have discovered that placing insulating materials just a few hundred nanometers from these tiny structures can dramatically increase energy loss, reducing their mechanical quality factor by as much as tenfold.

The findings, published in Nature Physics by scientists in the group of Tobias J. Kippenberg, identify a previously underappreciated limitation for ultrahigh-precision sensors and quantum technologies. The source of the problem is an electrical interaction that allows energy to escape across an otherwise empty gap.

The mechanism begins with static electric charges trapped inside a mechanical resonator. As the structure vibrates, those charges move with it, producing a changing electric field in the surrounding space. When an insulating material such as silicon dioxide or silicon nitride is nearby, the fluctuating field interacts with the material and causes energy to dissipate through its small electrical losses.

This process is related to “noncontact friction,” a phenomenon previously observed in atomic force microscopy. Although the surfaces never touch, mechanical energy is transferred away from the vibrating structure. The resulting damping lowers its quality factor, which measures how efficiently a resonator stores vibrational energy rather than losing it.

The researchers developed a theoretical model predicting that lower-frequency vibrations would experience greater energy losses. To test this, they studied silicon nitride strings suspended approximately 500 nanometers (0.00002 inches) above a dielectric layer. By measuring how quickly different vibrational modes decayed, they confirmed that the lowest-frequency modes suffered the strongest additional damping, consistent with the model.

A second experiment examined resonators designed for exceptionally high quality factors. The team positioned vibrating strings between photonic crystal cavities, with separations of only a few hundred nanometers (roughly 0.00001 inches). As the gaps narrowed, the quality factor declined sharply, sometimes falling by a factor of ten. The researchers also demonstrated that their modeling approach could reproduce the effects of trapped charges in these more complicated device geometries.

Nanomechanical resonators are microscopic vibrating components fabricated on chips, operating at frequencies from a few kilohertz to several gigahertz. Their sensitivity makes them useful for detecting extremely small changes in mass, force, temperature, and pressure. They also serve as components in radiofrequency filters and chip-based clocks. Advanced versions can even be used to prepare quantum states of comparatively large mechanical objects and investigate fundamental physics.

Many of these applications require resonators to operate extremely close to other structures, particularly when measuring motion or coupling mechanical vibrations to light and electrical systems. The EPFL results show that trapped charges and dielectric losses must be considered when designing such closely integrated devices, even when no physical contact occurs.

The same interaction could also have practical uses. By measuring how mechanical vibrations lose energy near insulating surfaces, researchers may be able to characterize electrical losses in thin films or develop controlled interactions between mechanical resonators and other electrical systems. Understanding these effects could help engineers preserve mechanical coherence while integrating increasingly sensitive resonators into complex quantum and sensing devices.

Reference: “Non-contact friction in ultracoherent nanomechanical resonators near dielectric materials” by Amirali Arabmoheghi, Alessio Zicoschi, Guillermo Arregui, Mohammad J. Bereyhi, Yi Xia, Nils J. Engelsen and Tobias J. Kippenberg, 7 July 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03350-z

Non-Contact Boundary Drag and Spatial Impedance Leaks

Recent research out of EPFL’s laboratories (led by Tobias J. Kippenberg’s group) has identified a hidden limitation affecting state-of-the-art nanomechanical resonators and quantum sensors. These ultra-sensitive nano-strings boast vanishingly low internal thermal noise and near-zero physical friction, yet scientists discovered that they experience unexpected energy losses. Even when surfaces never touch, the nano-strings interact with electrical and mechanical drag from nearby objects across empty microscopic gaps, causing their quality factor to plummet by up to a factor of ten.

Mainstream physics identifies this as non-contact electrical interaction and charge-trapping across empty boundaries. When evaluated through continuous field dynamics and the Torsion Hill Framework, this discovery highlights a critical baseline rule of spatial impedance:

The Illusion of Empty Space: Conventional engineering treats an empty gap as a total insulator—a void where mechanical and electrical fields terminate. Under field mechanics, space is a continuous medium. An adjacent static surface introduces an abrupt local spatial impedance profile (Z_T), meaning that a vacuum gap does not isolate a vibrating structure from surrounding boundary forces.

Non-Contact Boundary Drag as grad Z_T Interference: When a nano-string oscillates, its mechanical motion generates localized torsional and spatial pressure waves. If a nearby boundary introduces an un-optimized impedance mismatch, field energy bleeds across the gap. This leakage acts as an invisible aerodynamic brake, degrading the resonator’s coherence without physical contact.

Two-Layer Isolation (Ribbon Substrate & Surface Coating) – EPFL Laboratory Link: To protect these nanomechanical sensors, EPFL’s research parameters can be met by deploying a dual-layer boundary configuration along the surrounding chamber walls—strictly isolating the cavity walls rather than coating or covering the active vibrating sensor itself, which would add mass and destroy resonance. Remarkably, the same Kippenberg laboratory at EPFL exploring these non-contact boundary leaks is renowned for pioneering the ultra-precise dual-layer ribbon and surface-coating fabrications needed to decouple mechanical stress, smooth out local spatial impedance steps (delta Z_T), eliminate charge-trapping, and prevent field leakage across microscopic gaps.

The Limit of Precision: Whether observing macroscopic gravitational field sheets, strain-tuned altermagnets, or EPFL’s nanomechanical resonators, precision is never limited solely by internal material friction. It is governed by how effectively boundaries are managed to maintain rotational phase clearance (Omega_pi) and eliminate spatial impedance drag. #6431. What Will Politics Look Like on Other Planets? It's Likely to Be a Mishmash

When we make our home on other worlds, who will be in charge?

Will it be an emperor, like the main character in âDune: Part Three,â the final movie in a trilogy based on Frank Herbertâs sci-fi saga? Or a billionaire, like the space mogul who plays a key role in setting up a Mars base in âFor All Mankindâ? Or a rebel alliance, like the revolutionaries in âStar Warsâ and âThe Moon Is a Harsh Mistressâ?

Jacob Haqq Misra, an astrobiologist who literally wrote the book on space sovereignty, suggests that itâll be none of the above, at least during the initial phases of extraterrestrial expansion.

âYouâre going to have Earth cultures represented, and ideas about Earth governance represented, and what will emerge is sort of a mishmash legal framework of agreements for how to coexist peacefully,â he says in the latest episode of the Fiction Science podcast. âThatâs maybe not even so bad.â

During our podcast chat, Misra laid out what sounds like a sensible perspective on the future of space politics, based on earthly precedents rather than starry-eyed assumptions about the final frontier.

For more than a decade, SpaceX founder Elon Musk has talked up the prospect of building a city on Mars â and more recently, a base on the moon. But who would be in charge? Thatâs an open question even for Musk, who joked at a 2016 tech conference about being declared âking of Mars.â In a more serious vein, he said the future form of Martian government was likely to be âa direct democracy, not representative.â

âIt would be people voting directly on issues,â Musk said. âAnd I think thatâs probably better because the potential for corruption is substantially diminished in a direct vs. a representative democracy.â

Musk also had some novel ideas about the legislative process.

âIt should probably be easier to remove a law than create one,â he said. âI think thatâs probably good because laws have infinite life unless theyâre taken away. So, I think my recommendation would be something like, letâs say, 60% of people need to vote in a law, but at any point greater than 40% of people can remove it. And any law should come with a built-in sunset provision. If itâs not good enough to be voted back in, maybe it shouldnât be there.â

Misra, who is the chief operating officer and senior research investigator at Blue Marble Space, explains in detail why it wouldnât be that easy to create a Martian government in a book titled âSovereign Mars.â The reason has to do with the Outer Space Treaty, a nearly 60-year-old agreement signed by more than 110 nations, including the United States, China, Russia and all the other space powers.

The treaty declares that all nations have the right to use the moon and other celestial bodies for peaceful purposes, but also says no nation can claim sovereignty or ownership of extraterrestrial territory. Moreover, governments bear responsibility and legal liability for their national space activities, whether carried out by public agencies or private ventures. Which means the treaty would keep Elon Musk from being the king of Mars, even if SpaceX builds its own city.

At least thatâs the way Misra sees it. Robert Zubrin, the president of the nonprofit Mars Society, sees it differently. In his view, the treatyâs provisions mean the signatories âhave explicitly signed away their rights to interfere with Mars settlement.â But how long would it take for a Mars settlement to stand on its own, without governmental assistance?

âThere are a lot of challenges to living on Mars that make it more difficult,â Misra says. âAnd thatâs what I think is valuable about thinking about governance on Mars: not that itâs a place to start over, but itâs a way to challenge our ideas to the extreme. Maybe we never live on Mars full time, but we challenge our ideas and apply those back here on Earth.â

Misra sees plenty of earthly parallels to the sorts of issues raised by the prospect of space settlement, and they get the full treatment in âSovereign Mars.â

The author of âSovereign Marsâ is Jacob Haqq Misra, chief operating officer and senior research investigator at Blue Marble Space. (Book cover design by Karl Janssen; Mars photo via NASA / JPL-Caltech / ASU / MSSS; author photo courtesy of Jacob Haqq Misra)

For example, consider the Antarctic Treaty System, which was set up nearly 70 years ago. The 58-nation treaty puts a freeze (heh, heh) on territorial claims of sovereignty. Administrative decisions about international activities in Antarctica are made by a 29-nation grouping of consultative parties, assisted by a secretariat based in Argentina.

Will Antarctica become independent? Misra doesnât think so â and he thinks the same line of reasoning would apply to Mars, at least in the early days of Red Planet exploration and settlement.

âTo imagine a city of a million people on Mars â Iâm not saying it wonât happen, but itâs very difficult to do so,â Misra says. âWe donât have cities that big on Antarctica. There doesnât really seem to be an economically compelling reason for it, although thereâs a lot of science on Antarctica. â¦ So, the lesson from reality and from science fiction is: Donât forget that itâs really, really hard to live in these harsh places.â

The U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea serves as another instructive example. That treaty lays out principles for coordinating activities in the worldâs oceans â including the establishment of exclusive economic zones that extend 200 nautical miles beyond a nationâs territorial waters. Within those zones, each nation holds sovereign rights to resource extraction, energy production and research while still allowing for free navigation and overflight.

Even though the United States never ratified the Law of the Sea Treaty, it follows many of the treatyâs provisions due to pragmatic considerations. Misra thinks a similar sense of pragmatism will guide the settlement process on the moon and Mars.

For example, if the United States and China both establish bases at the moonâs south pole, they could agree to establish exclusive economic zones surrounding those settlements.

âI donât expect territorial conflict,â Misra says. âThe moon is really big. Itâs going to be a while before we run into the problem of two entities wanting to occupy the same place. I donât know of any regions of the moon that are so desirable that only one actor, one space agency, could get there to the exclusion of others.â

But Misra doesnât think thereâll be a new treaty to formalize a space governance system, or a new international authority along the lines of the United Earth Space Probe Agency in the fictional âStar Trekâ universe. The United Nations tried unsuccessfully to go down that road in 1979 with an international pact known as the Moon Treaty.

âItâs on the books,â Misra says. âIt has a number of signatories, but a very small number of signatories, none of which actually have their own independent launch capabilities. And so, many legal scholars consider it a dead treaty.â

Instead, Misra suspects that the worldâs space powers will find ways to âcooperate in space in a way that preserves their joint sovereignty.â

âI think there will be new multi-actor consortiums that have relevance,â he says. âThey might be outside the jurisdiction of the United Nations, for example, but they might be great things that arenât just driving forward profits for private entities. They might really reflect cooperation for science and exploration.â

What might that look like on the moon and Mars?

âProbably what would be likely is something similar to maybe a hybrid of Antarctic settlements and the way the International Space Station works,â Misra says. âIn Antarctica, there are various distances between the different outposts. Some might be closer than others, and each countryâs laws apply to that module,â he says.

The arrangements on the International Space Station are even more complicated, because each module hooked up to the outpost is the property of the nation that built the module. âYou get these weird agreements where, when data is transmitted from one section to the other, itâs actually governed by several different nationsâ laws along the way,â Misra says. âAnd if you are a Russian and you move down a couple of modules, youâre now a Russian visiting America.â

Thatâs likely to lead to a Martian mishmash. âI think you have to accept some degree of pluralism with what comes on Mars,â Misra says.

But does that mean space settlements will always be a mishmash? Not necessarily. There could be several ways to get around the Outer Space Treatyâs barriers to sovereignty. For example, an ambitious spacefaring nation could simply withdraw from the treaty, and then assert full sovereignty over the territory it controls. In 2011, space billionaire Robert Bigelow warned that China might do exactly that.

Another option would be for a company like SpaceX to move its base of operations (including its launch facilities) from the U.S. to a country that isnât a party to the Outer Space Treaty.

In âSovereign Mars,â Misra suggests a different route to extraterrestrial independence. The U.S. government, for example, could pass a law surrendering its territorial claim to an area under its control on the moon or Mars.

âIf you get the blessing from Congress, then youâve got the backing of a nation-state that says we agree with this long-term vision of establishing autonomy,â he says. âThere might be a discussion about it at the U.N., but you know, if I had to guess, if the United States did that, weâd hear about China doing something similar in a few years.â

When it comes to determining the long-term future of Martian governance, Misra actually agrees with Musk.

âWhat I think is, the Martians should decide,â Misra says. âIâm interested to see what they would think works, because it might be different models than what we come up with on Earth, simply because living on Mars is different than living anywhere here.â

More from Jacob Haqq Misra on space sovereignty:

In addition to his work as an astrobiologist and an expert on space sovereignty, Jacob Haqq Misra delves into the mysteries surrounding unidentified anomalous phenomena, or UAP. He is a member of the UAP Science Advisory Council and the lead author of a study suggesting that a group of six small objects seen in a video recorded from a military aircraft near Kuwait was a flock of birds. Misra is also on the editorial review board for Limina â The Journal of UAP Studies and one of the editors of a forthcoming book titled âThe Politics of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Science, Security and Society.â

âDune: Part Threeâ opens in U.S. theaters on Dec. 18.

#6430. NYC’s Hottest New Wine Bar Started With a DM Slide

An interview with the team behind El Camarón Peludo.

Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings.

Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar spent the last five years slinging tacos at breakneck pace to keep up with the lines at Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez and rowdy World Cup crowds at Socceria. Now the duo is slowing things down a bit for their first full-service restaurant El Camarón Peludo, a playful wine and seafood spot in the West Village where guests linger over mariscos.

At the tiny, walk-in-only restaurant, the menu fuses Mexican seafood dishes with Spanish influences and excellent wine from around the world. For the project, Cervantes and Apolinar teamed up with chef Carlos Barrera, a Mexico City-born chef who has worked in Michelin-starred restaurants in Spain and hosted dozens of popular pop-ups around NYC. When I sat down with Cervantes and Apolinar, I planned to pick their brains about how and why they manage four wildly popular (and very different) New York City restaurants. Then I learned how much El Camarón Peludo was the result of fate: If it weren’t for space constraints, a tapas-fueled trip, and a social media superfan, the duo may have had an entirely different restaurant on their hands.

Pre Shift: Where did the idea for El Camarón Peludo come from?

Tania Apolinar: When we were looking at [the space], we considered making it a taqueria, but because of the [long shape of the restaurant], it wouldn’t have worked for that concept. We knew we wanted to do something different, focused on seafood and wine.

Giovanni Cervantes: I was in conversation with Carlos about this idea to serve mariscos in New York when we saw the space. We didn’t know [at the time], but we were setting up the basis of the menu because we were talking about what we like and what we miss a lot [from Mexico]. We also talked about [our past trips] to Europe. We were really interested in how to match [the style of European tapas and wine bars] with what we do, which is the Mexican approach.

How did you connect with Barrera for the project?

Cervantes: Carlos was one of the first clients that we ever had in Taqueria Ramírez. We met basically through that and through Instagram. He was always commenting a lot...

Cervantes: Exactly. Sending the flame emoji. Then soon enough, we find out that we were neighbors because he lives in Greenpoint, so we started seeing each other more often.

Apolinar: Then we did a pop-up with him serving his famous Trompo Negro, which is like al pastor with [a smoky black spice paste that is widely used in Yucatán and surrounding regions], and that was the first time we actually connected in a working setup. We’re really aligned and happy with the partnership.

Can you tell me about how you balance Mexican and Spanish influences on the menu?

Cervantes: When we found the space, we knew it was the perfect setup to try something different. Then we made a trip to Europe and a trip to Mexico. After we came back from Europe, I think I was feeling very “Europeanized.” I remember having a conversation with Tanya and Carlos about making it even more Spanish, and both of them were like, “What?” And I’m glad they [pushed back], because we definitely found the right balance.

Apolinar: We’re talking about Mexican and Spanish, but in the end, it’s about the seafood and the freshness, the product that we really want to stand out. That’s why [we serve a] very simple gambas a la plancha, and the carpaccio has that approach as well, but then other more Mexican classics [like tostadas topped with tuna or aguachile] have more sauces and all of that.

Cervantes: And it’s not just the food. The influence that we took from different parts of Europe is the setup, the vibe, the size of the plates, the type of space. We want the space to feel cozy and friendly.

How is the service different from your other spots?

Cervantes: At Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez, it’s all about efficiency. Making it right, as fast as you can, and getting people in and out of the place. It’s nonstop volume. The consistency is awesome over there, and that’s [how we] measure that we’re making it right. Here it’s different. It’s more about the experience of the space and the music and the wine. [Our staff are] with these people for an hour or two, so you try to make it personal in a way. It feels different when you have that much time to see how people are enjoying the experience and transporting people to that world through what we’re doing. That’s comforting to me.

Now that you have four different restaurants around the city, how do you balance your time between them?

Cervantes: For Taqueria Ramírez, the very first one, we can sleep very well because almost everybody on the staff has been there since we opened. I’m just mentioning that because it’s all about building the right team because you can only be in one place at a time. Then at Carnitas, our partners [Yvon de Tassigny and Kari Boden] are really great and the plan was for them to be the day to day operators from the beginning. So right now we’re between El Cameron Peludo and Socceria because they’re the new babies and there’s a lot of work to do there.

Tania: It’s tiring, but at the end of the day, I’ve been enjoying it a lot. It’s nonstop but it feels rewarding to see the point of view of customers and make people feel happy and connect to them.
